DelayedRetry::DurableZset parks a delayed delivery in a sorted set, so the retry survives a crash and fires at its due time.

retry_after on a plain stream makes the runtime republish a copy after the delay, which a crash before the timer loses.
With asyncapi the generated document carries an x-ruststream-redis extension that says which structure carries a channel and how.
A stream channel reports its group, consumer, read mode and idle threshold; a list its acknowledgement; a channel its mode.
A channel a service publishes to reports where the publish lands, a key or a channel, with its delivery mode, expiry and envelope.
The server reports the host and port a client dials, with the scheme, credentials, database and query stripped.
RedisBroker connects a service to Redis or Valkey; standalone only records the URL, and the runtime connects it at startup.
credentials sets an ACL user and its password on every topology; password is the legacy AUTH with a password and no user.
RedisBroker::cluster takes seed nodes, of which one reachable node is enough; the client discovers the rest of the cluster.
credential_provider supplies the user and password on each AUTH or HELLO, so a rotated password reaches a running service.
default_group names the consumer group a bare #[subscriber("key")] reads through; without it such a subscription refuses to start.
RedisError is the one error type of the crate: connect, publish, subscribe, stream reads, shutdown, transactions and refused options.
from_pool wraps a fred Pool the service built itself, for client settings the broker's own builders do not reach.
pool sets how many connections publishes, settlements and handler commands share; each subscription reads on a connection of its own.
Each form has a prelude with its policy under the name Publish; ruststream_fred::prelude serves a file that mixes forms.
sentinel_credentials and sentinel_password log in to the sentinels with a pair of their own, apart from the data nodes.
RedisBroker::sentinel names the monitored primary and the sentinels that watch it; the client finds the primary through them.
Shutdown unblocks every read and closes every connection; a publisher used afterwards gets RedisError::ShutDown at once.
tls takes a TlsConnector or TlsConfig on any topology; a rediss or valkeys URL switches TLS on for a standalone server.
StreamContext gives a stream handler the entry id, the position that redelivers it, the consumer group and the group's seek handle.
A stream batch handler's context carries only the consumer group and the seek handle, which belong to the whole subscription.
Ctx<keys::ConsumerGroup> binds the consumer group a stream subscription reads through, on a single delivery or a batch.
Ctx<keys::FredPool> hands a handler the broker's fred connection pool on every form, for a command whose answer it needs now.
PubSubContext gives a channel handler the channel a message arrived on and whether a pattern matched it.
RedisList is a work queue: each entry goes to one consumer, and the simple form pops it with BRPOP and settles nothing.
processing names the list an entry waits on while handled; on a cluster both keys share one hash tag, or the subscription refuses to start.
recovery_zset starts a watchdog that returns entries a dead consumer left on its processing list, once idle min_idle.
reliable moves each entry to a processing list and removes it on ack, which makes the queue at-least-once.
.pipeline() settles a subscription in a window, and a handler queues its own Redis commands to leave with its acknowledgement.
.atomic() after .pipeline() wraps each delivery's commands and settle in MULTI and EXEC, so they apply together or not at all.
pipeline.bind(out) makes a slot's publishes join the delivery's round, so they leave only if the delivery is acknowledged.
RedisPipeline queues fred's commands, Lua through eval and evalsha, and any other command through custom; a reply is not read back.
A window flushes when the read's COUNT has settled, when nothing is outstanding, or when the subscription stops.
The InRound transform on the reply position puts a handler's reply into its delivery's round, after the commands it queued.
RedisGroupPosition names where a consumer group resumes: the oldest retained entry, the tail, or the entry after an id.
EntryId is a stream entry's milliseconds-sequence id; the EntryId key binds the id a delivery was read at.
A handler moves its group's cursor through the SeekHandle key; a delivery's Position key seeks back to that delivery.
start_at moves the group to a position before the first delivery, on every startup; the whole group moves, not one consumer.
RedisPublish, Publish in the stream prelude, appends each message to a stream with XADD.
A reply with no named policy writes each name the way this service reads it, and XADDs a name it does not read.
RedisListPublish, Publish in the list prelude, pushes with LPUSH and can re-arm a key expiry at every publish.
partition_key keys one message, so workers(n, by_key) on the consuming side keeps the order of messages sharing that key.
RedisPubSubPublish, Publish in the Pub/Sub prelude, sends with PUBLISH or SPUBLISH in the envelope it names.
RedisPubSub reads one channel; a message reaches only the subscribers connected when it is published, and nothing is settled.
buffer sets how many messages a channel subscription holds while its handler is busy; past it the oldest is lost with a warning.
RedisPubSubPattern reads every channel a glob matches; a retry copy needs a destination named at the mount site.
PubSubMode picks classic SUBSCRIBE and PUBLISH, broadcast to every node, or sharded SSUBSCRIBE and SPUBLISH, local to a slot.
RedisStream::new reads fresh entries off a stream through a consumer group, and each ack is an XACK.
claiming reads pending entries idle at least min_idle and the fresh tail in one XREADGROUP CLAIM call; it needs Redis 8.4.
reclaim reads only entries another consumer of the group fetched and never acked, idle at least min_idle, with XAUTOCLAIM.
StreamStart says where a consumer group starts when the subscription creates it: the beginning, the end, or after an id.
A key in #[subscriber] reads that stream through the broker's default group; a descriptor names the form and its settings.
A slice handler reads one XREADGROUP COUNT on a stream; a list or a channel builds its batch on the client up to the same size.
block sets how long one read waits on the server: the XREADGROUP BLOCK on a stream, the BRPOP or BLMOVE timeout on a list.
An envelope is how a message's headers travel beside its payload; the broker names one, and a descriptor or a publish policy names its own.

transaction hands back a value that owns its buffer, so several can be open at once and a double commit does not compile.

ruststream-fred is the Redis and Valkey broker for RustStream, built on the fred client. A service reads Redis Streams through consumer groups, a list as a work queue, or Pub/Sub channels, on a standalone server, a cluster or a sentinel set. The guides take a Redis service from installation to production.
This section draws how Redis delivers messages through streams, lists and Pub/Sub, where ruststream-fred sits between Redis and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.
What ruststream-fred costs on every message: throughput against the raw fred client, and instructions and allocations of its code.

The first chart runs each scenario three ways on a real Redis server. Raw client is a loop written by hand on fred. Broker crate is the same loop written on this crate: the broker, the subscription, the stream of deliveries and the ack, with no runtime. RustStream is the service a user writes, a #[subscriber] handler in an app. The first gap is what this crate costs over the client it wraps, and the second is what the runtime adds on top. Each loop is a bar from its best round to its slowest, with a dot at the best round and a notch at the median. The zero of the axis is the raw client's best round, and a dot right of zero is slower. A hollow dot is a loop whose difference from the raw client is smaller than the spread of the rounds. The table under the chart prints the best round with the median in parentheses. Three forms are measured, one per transport: a stream read through a consumer group that acknowledges every entry, a reliable list, and a Pub/Sub channel. Each runs against a standalone server, a cluster and a primary behind Sentinel. On the cluster the Pub/Sub row is sharded, SSUBSCRIBE and SPUBLISH, the form a cluster is used with.

The second chart counts what one message costs on the service's thread: instructions under callgrind and allocations under DHAT, in the steady state. Each scenario is a service on RedisBroker against the standalone server of the stand. The service runs on a single-threaded runtime, and fred drives its connections on the same thread, so the count holds the runtime, this crate, and fred writing the commands and parsing the replies. The server is another process and is not counted. Cold start is what connecting the pool, creating the group, opening the subscription and taking the first delivery cost once. A stream scenario reads a consumer group with XREADGROUP, settles with XACK and replies with XADD. A reliable list claims each entry with BLMOVE and settles it with LREM. A Pub/Sub scenario reads a channel or a pattern and settles nothing. A .pipeline() scenario sends the settles of a read together and its handler queues one INCR per delivery, and .pipeline().atomic() wraps each delivery's segment in MULTI and EXEC, as Window draws.

How ruststream-fred measures itself: the three loops, the run on a real Redis server, the broker-bound arithmetic and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on Redis.

One process runs each scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the messages. Raw client. A loop on fred: read, decode, acknowledge. Broker crate. This crate and nothing above it: the broker connects, a descriptor opens a subscription, and a loop pulls deliveries off its stream, decodes them and acks them. RustStream. The service a user writes: a #[subscriber] handler and the app around it. Everything else is equal across the three: the pool and its size, the consumer group and the consumer name, the read commands with their COUNT and BLOCK, the place of the ack, the decode into the same type, the payload bytes, the tokio runtime with four worker threads, and the binary. All three are fed by the same pipelined fred publisher, so what differs between them is on the consuming side. The body is 512 bytes of JSON.

The message count comes from a probe, which measures the raw loop's rate, so a measured run lasts at least five seconds on any machine. The window opens at the first delivery and closes when the last one is taken, in all three loops. The loops are interleaved: raw, crate, RustStream, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. A row is broker-bound when the raw client spent the run waiting on the socket. A probe times one EXISTS and its answer on each topology, and the round trip is published with the machine, so the arithmetic can be checked. Settling a stream entry or a list entry costs a command of its own, XACK or LREM, and on the loopback that round trip costs more than a delivery spends inside this crate. Those rows carry the mark. Pub/Sub settles nothing, and it is the row where the work above the socket shows.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, built without the testing feature. Messages are appended from another thread before the measured region opens, so producing them is not counted. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. A scenario runs over one delivery, then 1000, then 2000. The difference between the last two is the steady cost of a message, and the single delivery is the cold start. The server is real, so a count moves a little between runs. Over six runs the instruction totals of a scenario stayed within 0.4 percent of each other, and its allocations within a few blocks. Each allocation floor is the highest count seen plus a margin of 0.1 percent. just bench-code fails on an allocation above the floor a scenario declares, and, with --baseline=main, on more than two percent more instructions.

just bench The recipe starts the stand from docker-compose.test.yml, runs every scenario, stops the stand and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json. It takes about ten minutes and wants the machine to itself. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. The build profile is recorded in the document with the numbers. just bench-code The code count starts the same stand, counts the scenarios under valgrind against its standalone server, stops the stand and rewrites the code section of the same document. It needs valgrind, and installs the benchmark runner itself. just bench-code --save-baseline=main on main records a baseline, and just bench-code --baseline=main on a branch compares with it.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-fred measure, and what they do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, on one server. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: the transports do different work per message. The server runs on the same machine, on the host network, with persistence off. With no network latency and no disk, the same cost per message is a larger share of the time than it would be against a server across a network. Read the percentage as an upper bound on what a deployed service pays. A broker-bound row is one where the raw client waited on the socket for most of the run. The work of the crate and the runtime then happens inside that wait, and the difference comes out near zero. That is a lower bound on the cost, not a measurement of it. The Pub/Sub row is taken under a publisher that never waits for the consumer. Pub/Sub drops what a subscription is not there to take, so that row reports the deliveries a saturated subscription handles per second.
documents.s: The comparison against a raw client

documents.t: An instruction count holds the runtime, this crate and fred's work on the service's thread. It includes the framework's own cost; the core publishes that cost alone on its benchmarks page. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the difference between a run of 1000 deliveries and one of 2000. Connecting, creating the group and the first allocations behind them are the cold start, paid once.

A row is one consumer reading one key, a small body and a server on the loopback. It measures what a delivery costs inside this crate and the runtime over it, not what Redis can carry. The window of a run opens at the first delivery and closes when the last one is taken, alike in all three loops, so one acknowledgement of a run sits outside the number everywhere. The publish path is not in the comparison: all three loops share one publisher. The code chart counts a reply on the same stand. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, on a machine given to the run alone: the differences they show are smaller than the noise of a shared one.

The runtime above it is the same for every broker. Everything Redis-specific is in this crate: the descriptors of the three transports, what an acknowledgement means on each, where a retry copy goes, and the pipeline window. A descriptor resolves once, at startup, against the connected broker, and yields a subscriber. The subscriber is a stream of deliveries that the runtime polls. The runtime decodes each delivery, runs the handler and settles the delivery with its outcome. A publish policy pairs with the connected broker into a publisher. Each subscription reads on a client of its own, so a blocked read never holds up a publish. Publishes, settlements and the commands a handler sends share the pool. Lifecycle draws when each client opens and closes, and Path the way of one entry. The headers travel beside the payload in an envelope, a type the broker names and a descriptor or a publish policy overrides. By default a stream entry carries the payload in a field named _payload and each header in a field h:<name>, and a list entry and a channel message carry the headers in a binary frame around the payload. A delivery finds its payload without reading the headers and reads them when a handler first asks.

RedisBroker records configuration, connect opens the pool, each subscription opens a client of its own, and shutdown unblocks and closes them. The broker's three states as types, and what each transition does on Redisconnect(self)shutdown(self)BrokerOn RedisRedisBroker::standalone(url)ConnectedRedisBrokerClosedRedisBrokerconnections_closedConfiguration only,no I/OA pool of 4 connections:publishes, settlesEach subscription:its group created,a client of its ownSubscription dropped:CLIENT UNBLOCK, QUITWaits for every readclient, QUITs the poolA publisher or delivery that outlives the connectionanswers RedisError::ShutDown at once The diagram as text Broker: RedisBroker:: standalone(url); ConnectedRedisBroker; ClosedRedisBroker connections_closed On Redis: Configuration only, no I/O; A pool of 4 connections: publishes, settles; Each subscription: its group created, a client of its own; Subscription dropped: CLIENT UNBLOCK, QUIT; Waits for every read client, QUITs the pool RedisBroker:: standalone(url) → ConnectedRedisBroker: connect(self) ConnectedRedisBroker → ClosedRedisBroker connections_closed: shutdown(self) Configuration only, no I/O → A pool of 4 connections: publishes, settles A pool of 4 connections: publishes, settles → Each subscription: its group created, a client of its own Each subscription: its group created, a client of its own → Subscription dropped: CLIENT UNBLOCK, QUIT Subscription dropped: CLIENT UNBLOCK, QUIT → Waits for every read client, QUITs the pool A publisher or delivery that outlives the connection answers RedisError::ShutDown at once RedisBroker::standalone records the URL and does no I/O, as do cluster and sentinel, so the service's builder stays synchronous. The runtime connects the broker when the app starts. Connect turns the topology, the credentials and the TLS settings into a fred configuration, and opens a pool of pool connections, four by default. An unreachable server fails the start. A broker built with from_pool adopts the pool it was given and dials it here, unless the service connected it already. Publishes, settlements and the commands a handler sends go out on the pool. Each subscription opens a client of its own when it subscribes. A stream or list subscription reads on it, because a blocking read (XREADGROUP with BLOCK, BLMOVE, BRPOP) holds its connection until it returns, and a publish queued behind it would wait out the whole block interval. A Pub/Sub subscription receives its messages on it. A stream subscription creates its consumer group before it returns. When a subscription is dropped, its client sends CLIENT UNBLOCK on fred's side connection, which ends a read still blocked on the server, and then QUIT. A blocked pop left running would take the next entry for a subscription nobody reads. Every connection reconnects after the server drops it, backing off from 100 ms to 10 s, and a command issued meanwhile waits for it. Shutdown marks the connection closed, waits until every read client has closed, and sends QUIT to the pool. ClosedRedisBroker reports how many pool connections it closed. A publisher, a seeker or a delivery that outlives the connection checks the mark before it sends, and answers RedisError::ShutDown at once.

The way of one stream entry through a RustStream service: the append, the group read, the delivery, the handler, the reply and the XACK. A batch handler reads as many entries as its batch size instead. When the stream has nothing new, the read blocks for the subscription's block interval, five seconds by default. Each entry becomes a RedisMessage: the _payload field is the payload, and each h: field a header. The runtime decodes the payload and calls the handler. The reply is encoded and published with XADD on a pool connection, and the delivery settles after it. A list read and a Pub/Sub message take the same way from the delivery on, with the form's own settlement, which Settlement draws.

Redis carries messages three ways: a stream keeps entries for consumer groups, a list hands each entry to one consumer, a channel keeps nothing. A producer writes to a stream, a list and a channel, and each transport hands the message to its readers differentlyXADDLPUSHPUBLISHStreamkeeps every entryListuntil poppedChannelkeeps nothingGroupbillingGroupauditConsumerstake turnsClientAClientBJoins later:never sees itEach group readsevery entryEach entry goesto one consumer The diagram as text XADD → Stream keeps every entry LPUSH → List until popped PUBLISH → Channel keeps nothing Stream keeps every entry → Group billing Stream keeps every entry → Group audit List until popped → Consumers take turns Channel keeps nothing → Client A Channel keeps nothing → Client B Joins later: never sees it Each group reads every entry Each entry goes to one consumer A stream is an append-only log. XADD appends an entry under an id the server assigns, and the entry stays until the stream is trimmed. A consumer group reads the stream with a cursor of its own, so two groups each receive every entry. Inside one group, each entry goes to one consumer. Groups draws how a group tracks what it delivered. A list is a queue. A producer pushes with LPUSH, a consumer pops from the other end, and a popped entry is gone from Redis. Queues draws how a reliable list keeps an entry until its handler settles it. A channel stores nothing. PUBLISH pushes a message to the clients subscribed at that moment, and a client that subscribes later never sees it. Broadcast draws it. A service reads each transport through its own descriptor: RedisStream, RedisList and RedisPubSub. The handler is the same #[subscriber] function on all three. What an acknowledgement means differs, as Settlement draws.

Redis Pub/Sub pushes a message to the subscriptions connected when it is published, and keeps nothing for anyone else. Pub/Sub: a publish reaches the subscriptions connected at that moment, each through its client's bufferpublishPublisherPUBLISH newsChannel newskeeps nothingSubscription AconnectedSubscription BconnectedSubscribeslater:never sees itClient buffer32 by defaultHandlerA handler that falls behind its bufferloses the oldest messages The diagram as text Publisher PUBLISH news → Channel news keeps nothing: publish Channel news keeps nothing → Subscription A connected Channel news keeps nothing → Subscription B connected Subscription A connected → Client buffer 32 by default Client buffer 32 by default → Handler Subscribes later: never sees it A handler that falls behind its buffer loses the oldest messages A channel is a name, not a key: Redis stores nothing under it. PUBLISH pushes the message to every client subscribed to the channel at that moment. Redis calls this at-most-once delivery: a client that is not subscribed, or loses its connection, never gets the message (Pub/Sub). Each RedisPubSub subscription opens a client of its own and subscribes it. At startup, the subscribe step of a classic subscription finishes once a PING sent after SUBSCRIBE on the same connection has been answered, so a message published after the subscription opened reaches it. RedisPubSubPattern subscribes to a glob with PSUBSCRIBE and receives every channel that matches it. A message waits in the client's buffer until the handler takes it. The buffer holds 32 messages, fred's default, unless buffer sets another size. A subscription that falls behind loses the oldest messages and logs a warning with the channel and the count. Classic Pub/Sub sends every message to every node of a cluster. Sharded Pub/Sub, SSUBSCRIBE and SPUBLISH since Redis 7.0, assigns a channel to a hash slot and keeps its messages inside that shard. PubSubMode picks one, and a subscription in one mode does not receive what is published in the other. A Pub/Sub delivery has nothing to settle: ack and nack answer AckError::Unsupported.

A consumer group reads a stream with one cursor and keeps every entry it delivered and nobody acknowledged in its pending entries list. One consumer group over a stream: its cursor, its pending entries list, and the commands that move entries between thempoints atXREADGROUPXACKclaimStream orders, as group workers sees it1-0acked2-0acked3-0pending4-0pending5-0new6-0newCursor:last-delivered-idPending entries list:3-0 to c1, 4-0 to c2Consumer c1reads new entriesConsumer c2acknowledgesConsumer c3claims idle onesXGROUP SETID moves the cursor back or forward: a seek The diagram as text Stream orders, as group workers sees it: 1-0 acked; 2-0 acked; 3-0 pending; 4-0 pending; 5-0 new; 6-0 new Cursor: last-delivered-id → 4-0 pending: points at Consumer c1 reads new entries → Cursor: last-delivered-id: XREADGROUP Consumer c2 acknowledges → Pending entries list: 3-0 to c1, 4-0 to c2: XACK Consumer c3 claims idle ones → Pending entries list: 3-0 to c1, 4-0 to c2: claim XGROUP SETID moves the cursor back or forward: a seek XREADGROUP with the id > returns the entries past the group's cursor, its last-delivered-id, and moves the cursor. Each entry goes to the one consumer that read it. The group records the entry in its pending entries list (PEL) with that consumer, the time of the delivery and a delivery count. XACK removes it from the list. The entry stays in the stream: an acknowledgement is the group's bookkeeping, not a delete. The crate creates the group when the subscription starts, with XGROUP CREATE and MKSTREAM, so a stream that does not exist yet is created empty. A group that already exists is kept as it is. StreamStart decides where a new group's cursor starts. An entry whose consumer died stays in the list. Two commands hand it to another consumer once it has been idle for a given time. XAUTOCLAIM scans the list for such entries and transfers them; RedisStream::reclaim reads that way, and asks XPENDING for the delivery counts of what it claimed. On Redis 8.4 and later XREADGROUP takes a CLAIM option, which returns the idle entries first and then new ones in one call, each with its idle time and delivery count. RedisStream::claiming reads that way, and a claiming subscription refuses to start on an older server. XGROUP SETID moves the cursor. The crate's RedisGroupSeeker uses it, so a seek repositions the whole group, not one consumer. A read that was selected under the old cursor is discarded, and the next read starts from the new one. The commands are Redis's own: XREADGROUP, XACK, XAUTOCLAIM and XGROUP SETID.

A reliable list moves each entry to a processing list before the handler runs, and removes it from there when the handler settles. A reliable list: a claim moves the entry to the processing list, the outcome settles it there, and the recovery set returns orphansLPUSHBLMOVEdeliveredZADDorphans backProducerjobsjobs.processingRecovery setsorted by claim timeHandlerack:LREMretry: LPUSHback, then LREMdrop:LREMEach read first sweeps claims idle past min_idle back to the queue The diagram as text Producer → jobs: LPUSH jobs → jobs.processing: BLMOVE jobs.processing → Handler: delivered jobs.processing → Recovery set sorted by claim time: ZADD Recovery set sorted by claim time → jobs: orphans back Handler → ack: LREM Handler → retry: LPUSH back, then LREM Handler → drop: LREM Each read first sweeps claims idle past min_idle back to the queue A list is a queue: LPUSH adds at one end, a pop takes from the other, and the oldest entry leaves first. A popped entry is gone from Redis. A simple RedisList pops with BRPOP, so an entry whose handler fails or whose process dies is lost: delivery is at most once. A reliable list claims instead of popping. BLMOVE moves the entry from the queue to a processing list in one command, and the entry stays there while the handler runs. The processing list is <key>.processing unless the subscription names another. The outcome settles the entry on the processing list: LREM removes it, and a retry first pushes it back to the queue. Delivery is at least once. Redis describes the pattern under LMOVE. A list keeps no record of who took an entry or when, so a consumer that dies after its claim leaves the entry on the processing list. recovery_zset keeps that record. Every claim is added to a sorted set, scored by its time. Each read first sweeps the claims older than min_idle and moves each of their entries back to the queue with LREM and LPUSH, at most 128 per read. On a cluster both lists have to hash to one slot, because BLMOVE touches both keys. A subscription whose two keys land on different slots refuses to start. A hash tag such as {jobs} puts both on one slot, and the default processing key follows it.

What ack, retry, drop and retry_after become on a Redis stream, a reliable list, a simple list and Pub/Sub. The commands each outcome sends, per form: a stream, a claiming stream, a reliable list, and the forms with no acknowledgementOutcomeStreamClaimingReliableNo ackackXACKXACKLREMnotsupportedretryXADD copy,then XACKstayspendingLPUSH,then LREMnotsupporteddropXACKXACKLREMnotsupported The diagram as text Outcome: ack; retry; drop Stream: XACK; XADD copy, then XACK; XACK Claiming: XACK; stays pending; XACK Reliable: LREM; LPUSH, then LREM; LREM No ack: not supported; not supported; not supported The runtime settles each delivery with the outcome its handler returned, and the crate maps the outcome onto the form's own acknowledgement. A stream acknowledges with XACK in the subscription's group. A reliable list removes the entry from its processing list with LREM. A simple list and Pub/Sub have nothing to acknowledge, and settling there answers AckError::Unsupported. The settle commands go out on the pool, not on the subscription's read client. A retry on a stream appends a copy of the entry to the same stream, then acknowledges the original. A crash between the two leaves a duplicate, not a loss. A claiming subscription retries through the pending entries list instead. It appends and acknowledges nothing, and its next read claims the entry back once it has been idle for min_idle, under the same id, with a delivery count one higher. A reliable list pushes the entry back to its queue before it removes it from the processing list.

The three ways a stream subscription serves retry_after: a copy in the process, a copy in a Redis sorted set, or the entry left pendingRuntime copyDelay queueClaimingdelaydueidleretry_after(delay) on a stream entryXACK theoriginalCopy held inthe process:lost on a crashXADD the copywhen the timerfiresZADD the copy,then XACKIn Redis,scored by itsdue timeA read sweepsit: XADD backto the streamStays inthe pendingentries listClaimed backaftermin_idle The diagram as text Runtime copy: XACK the original; Copy held in the process: lost on a crash; XADD the copy when the timer fires Delay queue: retry_after(delay) on a stream entry; ZADD the copy, then XACK; In Redis, scored by its due time; A read sweeps it: XADD back to the stream Claiming: Stays in the pending entries list; Claimed back after min_idle retry_after(delay) on a stream entry → XACK the original retry_after(delay) on a stream entry → ZADD the copy, then XACK retry_after(delay) on a stream entry → Stays in the pending entries list XACK the original → Copy held in the process: lost on a crash Copy held in the process: lost on a crash → XADD the copy when the timer fires: delay ZADD the copy, then XACK → In Redis, scored by its due time In Redis, scored by its due time → A read sweeps it: XADD back to the stream: due Stays in the pending entries list → Claimed back after min_idle: idle Redis has no per-entry delay, so a stream subscription serves retry_after in one of three ways. By default the runtime acknowledges the original and holds a copy, which it publishes back to the stream when the delay is up. The copy's retry count is one higher. A crash before the timer fires loses it. delayed_retry with DelayedRetry::DurableZset keeps the copy in Redis. The copy is added to a sorted set, scored by its due time, and then the original is acknowledged. Each read first moves the copies that are due back onto the stream with XADD, at most 128 per read, so a delay is honoured to within one block interval. The scores are wall-clock milliseconds, so the clocks of the services that share a queue should agree. A claiming subscription leaves the entry pending, and its next read claims it back once min_idle has passed. A delay shorter than min_idle waits min_idle. A list and a Pub/Sub subscription take the runtime's copy, which goes back to the list or the channel. A pattern subscription names the destination of its copies at its mount site. A max_attempts cap counts attempts with one of two numbers, and the form decides which. The claiming and reclaim modes count with the server's delivery count from the pending entries list. Every other form counts with the retry-count header that the copies carry, which the delay queue raises on every round.

A pipelined subscription settles in a window: the deliveries of a read queue their side effects, and one flush sends them with the settles. One read of a pipelined stream subscription: each delivery queues a command, the outcome keeps or drops it, and one flush sends the restsettle onlyOne flush, one round tripEntry 1-0queues an INCRack:segment keptEntry 2-0queues an INCRdrop:segment droppedEntry 3-0queues an INCRack:segment keptINCR of 1-0INCR of 3-0XACK 1-0 2-0 3-0Under .atomic() each segment is MULTI, its commands,the delivery's own settle, then EXEC The diagram as text One flush, one round trip: INCR of 1-0; INCR of 3-0; XACK 1-0 2-0 3-0 Entry 1-0 queues an INCR → ack: segment kept ack: segment kept → INCR of 1-0 Entry 2-0 queues an INCR → drop: segment dropped drop: segment dropped → XACK 1-0 2-0 3-0: settle only Entry 3-0 queues an INCR → ack: segment kept ack: segment kept → INCR of 3-0 Under .atomic() each segment is MULTI, its commands, the delivery's own settle, then EXEC .pipeline() at the mount site opens a window over the subscription. Each delivery of a read takes a slot in it. What its handler queues through Ctx<keys::Pipeline> goes into the slot's segment, a fred pipeline opened at the first queued command. The handler does not see the command's reply. The outcome decides the segment: ack keeps it, and drop, retry and retry_after drop it. Each outcome sends the settle the form sends without a window. A delivery dropped unsettled sends no settle: its segment goes, and its entry stays pending. A window flushes when the settled deliveries reach the read's COUNT, when nothing is outstanding, or when the subscription stops. The flush sends the kept segments in the order they were committed, then the settles of the read in one pipeline, on a connection of the pool. A stream's settles leave as one XACK, and a reliable list's as one LREM per entry. Under load that is one round trip per read. .atomic() wraps each segment in MULTI and EXEC and puts the delivery's own settle inside it. The handler's side effects and its acknowledgement then take effect together. Redis has no rollback: a command that fails inside EXEC leaves the others executed (transactions). On a cluster every key of a segment has to share the slot of the subscription's key. A flush that fails is reported once on the delivery stream. On the forms that settle, an entry whose settle failed stays pending and is delivered again.

The parts of ruststream-fred a Redis service uses, one page per component: the broker (RedisBroker), its subscription descriptors for streams, lists and Pub/Sub, its publish policies, the pipeline window and the in-process Redis a TestApp test runs on.

What ack and nack do on each form: XACK on a stream, LREM on a reliable list, nothing on a simple list or a channel. A handler ends a delivery with an outcome: ack, retry or drop. The runtime settles the delivery with that outcome, and each form turns it into its own Redis commands. Form ack retry drop Stream XACK XADD of a copy, then XACK XACK Stream, claiming XACK the entry stays pending and comes back after min_idle XACK List, reliable LREM off the processing list LPUSH back onto the queue, then LREM LREM List, simple nothing nothing nothing Channel or pattern nothing nothing nothing On a stream a retry appends a copy and then acknowledges the original, so a crash between the two leaves a duplicate rather than a loss. The copy is a new entry with a new id. A claiming subscription retries through the pending entries list instead: nothing is appended, and the entry keeps its id and its delivery count. A simple list and Pub/Sub keep nothing to settle: the entry left Redis when it was popped, and a message is gone once it is pushed. An ack, a drop or a retry there reports AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs an ack / nack failed warning for each delivery. A retry there delivers nothing again, unless it is a retry_after or a cap is declared: both travel as a copy the runtime publishes.

A payment is charged, dropped when it is malformed, or retried when the gateway is busy. Macros Manual examples/redis_acknowledgement.rs /// One handler, three outcomes: the ack settles the entry, the drop settles it without a copy, /// the retry appends a copy to `payments` and settles the original. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("payments").group("billing"))] async fn charge(payment: &Payment, State(gateway): State<PaymentGateway>) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "malformed payment dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } match gateway.charge(payment).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge failed, retrying"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/redis_acknowledgement.rs /// One handler, three outcomes: the ack settles the entry, the drop settles it without a copy, /// the retry appends a copy to `payments` and settles the original. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), AppState> for Charge { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if payment.amount_cents <= 0 { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "malformed payment dropped"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if let Err(err) = ctx.state().gateway.charge(payment).await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "charge failed, retrying"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn payments() -> RedisStream { RedisStream::new("payments").group("billing") }

The claiming modes report Redis's delivery count and idle time as headers, and a cap reads that count. A consumer group counts how often it has handed out each pending entry. The two stream modes that claim entries, claiming and reclaim, put that count on every delivery in DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER. IDLE_MS_HEADER carries how long the entry had been pending, in milliseconds. A claiming delivery reports the attempts made before it, so a fresh entry carries zero for both headers. A reclaim delivery reports the count including itself. The runtime reads the same count through redelivery_count, which counts the current delivery in both modes. That is the count a max_attempts cap reads. An entry a crashed worker took and never settled counts towards the cap, although no process saw it fail. A reclaiming read that found entries issues one XPENDING to learn their counts. Every other subscription has no count from Redis, and its cap counts through the runtime's retry-count header instead.

The handler logs both values with every attempt. Macros Manual examples/redis_acknowledgement_counts.rs /// A claimed entry carries how often Redis has handed it out before and how long it sat pending; /// the handler logs both with every attempt. #[subscriber(RedisStream::claiming("payouts", MIN_IDLE).group("payouts"))] async fn pay( payout: &Payout, ctx: &mut Context<'_>, State(gateway): State<PaymentGateway>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let earlier = ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); let idle_ms = ctx.headers().get_str(IDLE_MS_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); tracing::info!(payout.id, earlier, idle_ms, "paying out"); match gateway.pay(payout).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(err) => { tracing::warn!(payout.id, %err, "payout failed, left pending"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } } } examples/manual/redis_acknowledgement_counts.rs /// A claimed entry carries how often Redis has handed it out before and how long it sat pending; /// the handler logs both with every attempt. struct Pay; impl Handle<Payout, (), (), (), AppState> for Pay { async fn handle( &self, payout: &Payout, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let earlier = ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); let idle_ms = ctx.headers().get_str(IDLE_MS_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); tracing::info!(payout.id, earlier, idle_ms, "paying out"); if let Err(err) = ctx.state().gateway.pay(payout).await { tracing::warn!(payout.id, %err, "payout failed, left pending"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } fn payouts() -> RedisStream { RedisStream::claiming("payouts", MIN_IDLE).group("payouts") } The cap at the mount site reads the same count: the third failed delivery goes to payouts.dlq. max_attempts(n) caps deliveries and dead_letter(name) names where a spent message goes, written with its own form's command. Both are steps of the mount chain, and they read the same on a stream, a list and a channel. max_attempts(n) counts every delivery of one message, the first one included. When the n-th delivery asks for a retry, the runtime settles it and publishes it to the dead-letter name instead, payload and headers as they arrived. The name is written the way the source form writes: XADD from a stream, LPUSH from a list, PUBLISH from a channel. A cap without a dead-letter name drops the spent delivery and logs a warning that names the subscription. A dead-letter name without a cap carries every retry away on the first one. Under a cap an immediate retry travels as a copy the runtime publishes, so that the count moves with the message in RETRY_COUNT_HEADER. A claiming subscription reads Redis's own delivery count instead and appends nothing. Redis keeps a delivery count only in a stream's pending entries list, which the claiming and reclaim modes read. On a list, a channel and a plain stream read, the runtime applies the cap with the count its copies carry. The dead-letter key is an ordinary key of the same broker, and a subscription reads it like any other. A name one subscription reads as one Redis type and another writes as a second type stops the service at startup, and the error names both.

DelayedRetry::DurableZset parks a delayed delivery in a sorted set, so the retry survives a crash and fires at its due time. A stream subscription takes it with RedisStream::delayed_retry. A retry_after then adds the entry to the sorted set with ZADD, scored by its due time, with its retry count raised by one. The original is acknowledged with XACK once the entry is parked. Each read of the subscription sweeps the set and appends the entries that are due back onto the stream, each under a new id. Nothing about the delay lives in the service, so a restart or a crash loses no retry. The sweep runs once per read, so the block interval sets how late a due entry may come back, and one pass moves at most 128 entries. Scores are wall-clock epoch milliseconds, so the clocks of the services that share a set have to agree. ttl expires a set no retry has refreshed for that long, and it has to exceed the longest delay, or entries are dropped before they are due. The set costs keys, memory and a sweep, so a subscription has it only when its descriptor names it. On a claiming subscription the set honours the delay as asked, instead of rounding it to min_idle.

Each descriptor names where a retry copy goes; a pattern names none, so its registration names the channel with out_retry. The runtime publishes a copy for a retry_after, for a retry under a cap, and for a dead letter. A stream, a list and a channel subscription each answer with their own key or channel, so the copy reaches the same subscription again. A copy leaves through RedisDefaultPublish unless the registration names another policy. That publisher writes a name the way the service reads it: XADD to a stream, LPUSH to a list, PUBLISH to a channel in its mode, each in the envelope the subscription reads. .out_retry(policy) replaces the policy, and .transform(..) after it changes each copy on its way out. A pattern reads many channels and names none a PUBLISH can reach. Its registration names the channel with .out_retry(policy).to(channel), or mounts a publish transform that declares Destination = Names and names one per delivery. A pattern registration that names neither does not start, and the error names the subscription and both fixes.

retry_after(delay) on a plain stream makes the runtime republish a copy after the delay, which a crash before the timer loses. Redis has no per-message delay, so the runtime serves it. It settles the delivery, holds the payload and headers in memory, and publishes a copy once the delay is up. The copy goes where the subscription's descriptor says a copy goes: the stream key, the list key or the channel, and for a pattern the channel its registration names. It carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER one higher than the delivery it replaces. The copy waits in the service's memory, so it is at most once over the delay: a process that exits before the timer fires loses it. A simple list and Pub/Sub settle nothing, and they get the copy all the same. The copy leaves through the registration's retry publisher, which out_retry replaces. A stream that has to keep the delayed message across a crash parks it in Redis with DelayedRetry. A claiming subscription keeps the entry pending instead, so the delay rounds up to its min_idle, and a longer delay is not held that long.

With the asyncapi feature the generated document carries an x-ruststream-redis extension that says which structure carries a channel and how. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. The specification has a redis binding, but its objects carry no fields, and a binding key is a closed list. So this crate writes an extension instead, x-ruststream-redis, at the level a binding sits at. The server reports the host and port clients dial. A channel a service reads reports the Redis structure behind it and how the subscription reads it. A channel a service publishes to reports where the publish lands and how. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the broker, the descriptors, the policies and the destinations the mount sites resolved. The Redis server's version stays out, because the client learns it only in the handshake. The document is published and shared, so it carries no credential. The binary #[ruststream::app] writes prints the document with asyncapi gen. This crate's asyncapi feature turns on the core's asyncapi feature with it. The core's feature alone produces a document without the extension.

The dependency line: ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label redis, the key of its server in the document. cargo run --example redis_asyncapi --features asyncapi -- asyncapi gen prints the document. A stream channel reports its group, consumer, read mode and idle threshold; a list its acknowledgement; a channel its mode. Each channel a service reads carries form, the Redis structure behind it: stream, list or pubsub. The rest of the extension is the descriptor's own settings. Form Fields stream group, consumer, readMode (fresh, reclaim or claiming), minIdleMs for the two modes that claim, envelope list reliable, processing (the processing list of a reliable list), envelope pubsub mode (classic or sharded), pattern, envelope A RedisPubSubPattern channel reports pattern: true, so a reader knows the address is a glob and not a channel to publish to. envelope.contentType is the media type of the value the envelope writes: application/octet-stream for a binary frame, the codec's media type for a codec document. A setting the descriptor leaves to the broker, such as a consumer name it did not set, stays out.

The channel orders reports a claiming read in the group workers, as the consumer worker-1, from thirty seconds of idle time. The channel jobs reports a reliable list, and events a sharded channel. A channel a service publishes to reports where the publish lands, a key or a channel, with its delivery mode, expiry and envelope. The publish policy describes the channel, in the word Redis uses for the destination. A stream publisher reports the key it appends to and its envelope. A list publisher reports its key, the ttlMs every push re-arms, and its envelope. A Pub/Sub publisher reports its channel, the mode it publishes in, and its envelope. The destination is the one the mount site resolved: a reply("..") clause, a reply type's #[outgoing(name)], or an entry of a slot. So a reply declared with reply("orders.done") reports orders.done, whichever subscription produced it. A dead-letter destination is reported as a channel the service publishes to.

The reply of orders goes out on the Pub/Sub channel orders.done. The reply of jobs goes to the list jobs.done, which expires a minute after the last push. The server reports the host and port a client dials, with the scheme, credentials, database and query stripped. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. Its protocol is redis. Its host is the host:port of a standalone URL, or the first seed of a cluster or a sentinel list. A redis:// or rediss:// scheme, a user:password@, a /2 database and a ? query stay out of it. An address without a port reports the topology's default, 6379, or 26379 for a sentinel. A broker built with from_pool reports no host at all. Its address sits inside the pool's own config, and an empty host would read as an address to dial. A password set with credentials never reaches the document either.

The broker's URL carries a password and a database. Its server in the document is redis.internal:6379 with the protocol redis. RedisBroker connects a service to Redis or Valkey; standalone only records the URL, and the runtime connects it at startup. standalone takes the URL of one server, such as redis://localhost:6379. The URL may carry a user and password (redis://user:pass@host:6379) and a database number (/2). A rediss:// or valkeys:// URL switches TLS on. The constructor does no I/O, so the whole service fits the synchronous #[ruststream::app] builder. A cluster, a Sentinel deployment and a pool the service built have constructors of their own. The settings that follow are builder steps too: the pool size, the default consumer group and the credentials. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedRedisBroker. The connect opens the pool and waits for it, so an unreachable server fails startup instead of the first publish. Every subscription and every publisher of the service opens against that connected form. At shutdown the runtime turns it into a ClosedRedisBroker. Every connection the broker opens reconnects after the server drops it, with no limit on the attempts. The first attempt follows after 100 ms, and each next one twice as late, at most 10 s apart. A command issued while the connection is down waits for it. A Pub/Sub subscription subscribes again. A consumer group the server lost is created again and reads the stream from its start.

The client logs in on every connection it opens, the subscriptions' own included, and again after each reconnect. credentials names an ACL user, which Redis 6 and later and Valkey check against the user's rules. password logs in as the default user, the form a server configured with requirepass expects. A cluster seed list and a sentinel list carry no password, so credentials is how those topologies log in. A login the server refuses fails startup. The generated document never carries the password. A password that changes while the service runs comes from a credential_provider.

RedisBroker::cluster takes seed nodes, of which one reachable node is enough; the client discovers the rest of the cluster. Each seed is a host:port address, and a seed without a port means 6379. At startup the client reads the slot map from the first seed that answers. From then on it sends each command to the node that owns its key's hash slot. A cluster seed list carries no password, so a cluster that requires one takes credentials. Redis refuses a command or a transaction whose keys live in different hash slots. So the transactional policy TransactionalPublish refuses a cluster, and a service that names it does not start. A reliable list moves an entry between its queue and its processing list in one command, so both keys need one slot. A hash tag gives them one: in {jobs} and {jobs}.processing only jobs is hashed. A reliable list whose two keys hash apart refuses to start, and the error names the hash tag that fixes it. In #[outgoing(name = "..")] braces mark a name template, so a type published to a tagged key declares no name, and the call site names the key. A TestApp test runs a cluster service in process. The in-process Redis keeps the cluster topology and refuses what spans hash slots, as a cluster does.

The service works a reliable list under the hash tag {jobs} and reaches the cluster through two seeds. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_cluster.rs /// The hash tag `{jobs}` keeps the queue and its processing list `{jobs}.processing` on one node. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("{jobs}").reliable())] async fn run_job(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "job done"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(run_job)) } /// Two seeds: the client reaches the cluster through whichever answers first. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::cluster([ "redis-1.internal:6379", "redis-2.internal:6379", ])) } examples/manual/redis_broker_cluster.rs struct RunJob; impl Handle<Job> for RunJob { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "job done"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The hash tag `{jobs}` keeps the queue and its processing list `{jobs}.processing` on one node. fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber(RedisList::new("{jobs}").reliable(), RunJob).build()) }) } /// Two seeds: the client reaches the cluster through whichever answers first. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::cluster([ "redis-1.internal:6379", "redis-2.internal:6379", ])) }

credential_provider supplies the user and password on each AUTH or HELLO, so a rotated password reaches a running service. A provider implements CredentialProvider, fred's trait re-exported by the crate. Its fetch returns the user and the password, and the client calls it before every login: at startup, on each new connection and after each reconnect. Its refresh_interval makes the client log in again on a schedule, so a short-lived password is replaced before it expires. The provider wins over credentials set on the same broker. The trait is asynchronous through async-trait, so the service depends on that crate too. It comes with the credential-provider feature. A TestApp test runs no handshake, so the provider is not called there.

The dependency lines: ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["credential-provider"] } async-trait = "0.1" The provider reads the password of the user worker from a secret file the platform rotates, and logs in again every ten minutes. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_credential_provider.rs /// The password of the ACL user `worker`, read from a secret file the platform rotates. #[derive(Debug)] struct RotatedSecret { path: PathBuf, } #[async_trait] impl CredentialProvider for RotatedSecret { async fn fetch( &self, _server: Option<&Server>, ) -> Result<(Option<String>, Option<String>), FredError> { let path = self.path.clone(); // A file read blocks, so it runs off the connection's task. let read = task::spawn_blocking(move || fs::read_to_string(path)) .await .map_err(|err| FredError::new(ErrorKind::Auth, err.to_string()))?; let password = read.map_err(|err| FredError::new(ErrorKind::Auth, err.to_string()))?; Ok((Some("worker".to_owned()), Some(password.trim().to_owned()))) } /// Logs in again every ten minutes, with whatever the file holds by then. fn refresh_interval(&self) -> Option<Duration> { Some(Duration::from_mins(10)) } } fn broker(url: &str, secret: PathBuf) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::standalone(url).credential_provider(Arc::new(RotatedSecret { path: secret })) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker( "redis://localhost:6379", PathBuf::from("/run/secrets/redis-password"), )) } examples/manual/redis_broker_credential_provider.rs /// The password of the ACL user `worker`, read from a secret file the platform rotates. #[derive(Debug)] struct RotatedSecret { path: PathBuf, } #[async_trait] impl CredentialProvider for RotatedSecret { async fn fetch( &self, _server: Option<&Server>, ) -> Result<(Option<String>, Option<String>), FredError> { let path = self.path.clone(); // A file read blocks, so it runs off the connection's task. let read = task::spawn_blocking(move || fs::read_to_string(path)) .await .map_err(|err| FredError::new(ErrorKind::Auth, err.to_string()))?; let password = read.map_err(|err| FredError::new(ErrorKind::Auth, err.to_string()))?; Ok((Some("worker".to_owned()), Some(password.trim().to_owned()))) } /// Logs in again every ten minutes, with whatever the file holds by then. fn refresh_interval(&self) -> Option<Duration> { Some(Duration::from_mins(10)) } } fn broker(url: &str, secret: PathBuf) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::standalone(url).credential_provider(Arc::new(RotatedSecret { path: secret })) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker( "redis://localhost:6379", PathBuf::from("/run/secrets/redis-password"), )) }

default_group names the consumer group a bare #[subscriber("key")] reads through; without it such a subscription refuses to start. A bare name subscribes to the stream under that key and reads its fresh entries. Redis reads a stream only through a consumer group, and a bare name names none. The broker's default group supplies it, for every bare name of the broker. A subscription created at startup creates its group too, so the stream and the group need not exist beforehand. Without a default group the service does not start. The error is RedisError::InvalidOptions, and its message names the key and the setting. A RedisStream descriptor names its group itself, and the default group does not apply to it.

The handler reads the stream orders by its bare name, in the group workers. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_default_group.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn take(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(take)) } /// Every bare-name subscription of this broker reads in the group `workers`. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers")) } examples/manual/redis_broker_default_group.rs struct Take; impl Handle<Order> for Take { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(subscriber("orders", Take).build())) } /// Every bare-name subscription of this broker reads in the group `workers`. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers")) }

RedisError is the one error type of the crate: connect, publish, subscribe, stream reads, shutdown, transactions and refused options. Each variant names the step that failed. The fred error behind it is its source, so the client library's types stay out of the crate's API. Variant When Connect the address could not be parsed, the server did not answer, or the login was refused Publish the server refused a write, such as a list push to a key that holds a stream (WRONGTYPE) Subscribe a consumer group could not be created, or a subscription could not open Stream a stream read or an acknowledgement failed ShutDown a publisher, a delivery or a transaction was used after the broker shut down InvalidOptions the settings cannot work together, such as a bare name with no default group ServerTooOld a claiming subscription met a server older than Redis 8.4 TransactionBusy, NoTransaction a transaction was begun twice on one publisher, or ended with none open Flush a pipelined window failed to send what it owed A service meets the error in two places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads anything. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how the delivery settles. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

A ledger entry the server refuses is logged with its cause, and the order is settled as a retry. The subscription claims the order back once it has been idle thirty seconds. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_errors.rs /// A retried order stays pending and comes back once it has been idle for thirty seconds. #[subscriber(RedisStream::claiming("orders", Duration::from_secs(30)).group("workers"))] async fn book(order: &Order, Out(ledger): Out<impl Publisher, Ledger>) -> HandlerOutcome { let entry = LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id, amount: order.amount, }; if let Err(err) = ledger.message(&entry).publish().await { // The error carries the server's answer, such as `WRONGTYPE`. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "ledger entry not written"); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_broker_errors.rs struct Book; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Book where Entry: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let entry = LedgerEntry { order_id: order.id, amount: order.amount, }; if let Err(err) = outs.get(Ledger).message(&entry).publish().await { // The error carries the server's answer, such as `WRONGTYPE`. tracing::warn!(subscription = "orders", order.id, error = %err, "ledger entry not written"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } /// A retried order stays pending and comes back once it has been idle for thirty seconds. fn orders() -> RedisStream { RedisStream::claiming("orders", Duration::from_secs(30)).group("workers") }

RedisBroker::from_pool wraps a fred Pool the service built itself, for client settings the broker's own builders do not reach. fred's Builder sets what the broker leaves at fred's defaults: a command timeout, a reconnection policy, buffer sizes, any topology a fred Config describes. The service builds the pool in its #[ruststream::app] builder and hands it over unconnected. The broker dials it when the service starts, and an unreachable server fails the start, as it does for a broker built from an address. A pool the service has already connected is adopted as it is. The pool's size is the pool of the broker. Each subscription's own connection is built from the pool's config and reconnects by the pool's policy. The generated document reports no host for such a broker, because the address sits inside the pool's own config. A TestApp test runs the same app in process: it reads the pool's size and config and dials nothing.

The dependency line: fred = "10" The pool holds eight connections, bounds every command at two seconds and reconnects every half second. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_from_pool.rs /// Eight connections, a two-second bound on every command, and a reconnect every half second. fn pool(url: &str) -> Result<Pool, FredError> { Builder::from_config(Config::from_url(url)?) .with_performance_config(|performance| { performance.default_command_timeout = Duration::from_secs(2); }) .set_policy(ReconnectPolicy::new_constant(0, 500)) .build_pool(8) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { // A constant URL and a non-zero size: the pool always builds. let pool = pool("redis://localhost:6379").expect("a pool over a valid URL"); // The pool is not connected here: the broker dials it when the service starts. service(RedisBroker::from_pool(pool)) } examples/manual/redis_broker_from_pool.rs /// Eight connections, a two-second bound on every command, and a reconnect every half second. fn pool(url: &str) -> Result<Pool, FredError> { Builder::from_config(Config::from_url(url)?) .with_performance_config(|performance| { performance.default_command_timeout = Duration::from_secs(2); }) .set_policy(ReconnectPolicy::new_constant(0, 500)) .build_pool(8) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { // A constant URL and a non-zero size: the pool always builds. let pool = pool("redis://localhost:6379").expect("a pool over a valid URL"); // The pool is not connected here: the broker dials it when the service starts. service(RedisBroker::from_pool(pool)) }

pool sets how many connections publishes, settlements and handler commands share; each subscription reads on a connection of its own. The pool holds 4 connections unless the service sets another number. Replies, acknowledgements, retries and the commands a handler sends through FredPool take turns on them. Each stream and list subscription reads on one more connection, and each Pub/Sub subscription listens on one. So a blocking read never holds up a publish, and a service opens the pool plus one connection per subscription. A pool of zero connections fails startup. A TestApp test keeps the pool size, and refuses zero the same way.

The service answers each order with a receipt through a pool of sixteen connections. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_pool.rs /// Sixteen pooled connections for the replies and acknowledgements of a busy service. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").pool(16)) } examples/manual/redis_broker_pool.rs /// Sixteen pooled connections for the replies and acknowledgements of a busy service. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").pool(16)) }

Each form has a prelude with its policy under the name Publish; ruststream_fred::prelude serves a file that mixes forms. A service on one form globs that form's prelude: stream::prelude, list::prelude or pubsub::prelude. Each carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds RedisBroker, the form's descriptors and their options, the form's context types, and the capabilities the form offers. The form's policy comes under the name every broker crate uses, Publish, so a mount site reads the same on every broker. The stream prelude also brings TransactionalPublish, the seek types and the keys module of context keys. ruststream_fred::prelude is for a file that mixes forms. It holds the same items for all three forms, with the policies under their prefixed names, RedisPublish, RedisListPublish and RedisPubSubPublish. It also brings the stream, list and pubsub modules, so a mixed file writes stream::Publish beside pubsub::Publish. It has no bare Publish, because one name would stand for three types. A handler body names only the capability it needs, such as Out<impl Publisher>, so moving a handler between forms changes the descriptor and not the handler. The one exception is a body that sets a per-message setting: it names RedisPublishOptions in its bound, from this crate's prelude.

A stream subscription replies onto a Pub/Sub channel, and a channel subscription hears the reply. The one glob brings both descriptors and the pubsub module the reply policy comes from. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_fred::prelude::*; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipped { order_id: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), reply)] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> Shipped { Shipped { order_id: order.id } } #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("shipments"))] async fn notify(shipped: &Shipped) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipped.order_id, "customer notified"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // Each form's policy under its module: `stream::Publish`, `list::Publish`, `pubsub::Publish`. b.include(ship) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::new()) .include(notify) }, ) } examples/manual/redis_broker_prelude.rs use ruststream_fred::prelude::*; struct Ship; impl Handle<Order, Shipped> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shipped, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Shipped { order_id: order.id })) } } struct Notify; impl Handle<Shipped> for Notify { fn handle( &self, shipped: &Shipped, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipped.order_id, "customer notified"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // Each form's policy under its module: `stream::Publish`, `list::Publish`, `pubsub::Publish`. b.include( subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), Ship) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::new()) .include(subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("shipments"), Notify).build()) }, ) }

sentinel_credentials and sentinel_password log in to the sentinels with a pair of their own, apart from the data nodes. A Sentinel deployment may protect the sentinels and the primary separately. The client asks the sentinels where the primary is, logged in with sentinel_credentials, and then logs in to the primary with credentials. sentinel_password is the form with a password and no user. Both come with the sentinel-auth feature and apply to the sentinel topology only. A TestApp test runs no handshake, so it proves the service starts and works with both pairs set.

The dependency line: ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["sentinel-auth"] } The primary checks the user worker, and the sentinels the user monitor. RedisBroker::sentinel names the monitored primary and the sentinels that watch it; the client finds the primary through them. The first argument is the name the sentinels monitor the primary under, such as mymaster. The second is the sentinels, each a host:port address; a sentinel without a port means 26379. At startup the client asks the sentinels where the primary is and connects to it. Every read and every write goes to the primary. After a failover the connections reconnect, and the client asks the sentinels again, so the service follows the new primary. A sentinel list carries no password. The primary's password goes in credentials, and the sentinels' own in sentinel_credentials.

The service reaches the primary mymaster through either of two sentinels. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_sentinel.rs /// The primary `mymaster`, found through either of two sentinels. fn broker() -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::sentinel( "mymaster", ["sentinel-1.internal:26379", "sentinel-2.internal:26379"], ) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) } examples/manual/redis_broker_sentinel.rs /// The primary `mymaster`, found through either of two sentinels. fn broker() -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::sentinel( "mymaster", ["sentinel-1.internal:26379", "sentinel-2.internal:26379"], ) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker()) }

Shutdown unblocks every read and closes every connection; a publisher used afterwards gets RedisError::ShutDown at once. When the service stops, the runtime runs the on_shutdown hooks while the broker is still connected and then shuts the broker down. A stream or list subscription may be waiting in a blocking read on its own connection. The broker sends CLIENT UNBLOCK for each such read, so the read ends at once instead of at its timeout, and closes the connection. Then the pool sends QUIT on every connection, and the after_shutdown hooks run. A publisher taken before the shutdown keeps pointing at the closed connection. A publish through it, an acknowledgement of a delivery or a transaction returns RedisError::ShutDown, and never runs against the dead pool. A tool that drives the broker by hand receives a ClosedRedisBroker from the shutdown; its connections_closed is the number of pooled connections it closed.

The service answers each order with a shipment, and logs once its connections are closed. Macros Manual examples/redis_broker_shutdown.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(ship) }) // Runs once every connection of the broker is closed. .after_shutdown(async move |_state| { tracing::info!("redis connections closed"); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) } examples/manual/redis_broker_shutdown.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("workers"), Ship) .reply() .build(), ) }) // Runs once every connection of the broker is closed. .after_shutdown(async move |_state| { tracing::info!("redis connections closed"); Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) }

tls takes a TlsConnector or a TlsConfig on any topology; a rediss:// or valkeys:// URL switches TLS on for a standalone server. TLS comes with one of three features, all off by default. tls-rustls builds on rustls with the aws-lc-rs crypto provider, tls-rustls-ring on rustls with ring, and tls-native-tls on the platform's own TLS library. The features add to each other rather than exclude each other. The crate re-exports TlsConnector and TlsConfig from fred, so a service names them without a dependency on fred. TlsConnector::default_rustls() trusts the system's root certificates and presents no client certificate. It reads the certificates from the system and can fail, so the connector is built in main before the service starts. A connector built from a rustls ClientConfig carries a private certificate authority or a client certificate. Every connection of the broker uses it, the subscriptions' own included. A TestApp test runs no handshake, so it proves the service starts and works with the connector in place.

The dependency line: ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["tls-rustls"] } The service reaches a cluster over TLS and logs in as the ACL user worker. StreamContext gives a stream handler the entry id, the position that redelivers it, the consumer group and the group's seek handle. The subscription builds it once per delivery, beside the payload and the headers. A handler names it as its context type, ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, and reads a field with ctx.context(key). A handler that needs one field binds it as a parameter with Ctx<K> instead. Each key is a type in context::keys, and the stream prelude brings the module in as keys: Key Value What it is EntryId EntryId the <milliseconds>-<sequence> id the entry was read at; it orders the way the stream does Position RedisGroupPosition the group cursor that delivers this entry again ConsumerGroup &str the group the subscription reads through, as ConsumerGroup shows SeekHandle RedisGroupSeeker the handle that moves the whole group to another position FredPool fred::clients::Pool the broker's connection pool, as FredPool shows Each key is a zero-sized type, and reading it is a plain field access the compiler resolves: no hashing, no boxing, no downcast. A key belongs to the context types that carry its field, so a key read off the wrong form's context does not compile. A batch handler reads StreamBatchContext, a Pub/Sub handler PubSubContext. A list delivery carries its payload and headers alone; a list handler reads the pool through FredPool or keeps the default () context. The two claiming read modes report a delivery's count and idle time as the DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER and IDLE_MS_HEADER headers, which every transport reads the same way. A context costs a handler that does not name one nothing: the default () context builds no value.

The handler writes where each order sat in the stream, and which group read it, to an order trail. Macros Manual examples/redis_context_stream.rs /// Reads the entry id and the consumer group off the delivery's context. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("audit"), reply)] async fn trace(order: &Order, ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>) -> Trail { let entry_id = ctx.context(keys::EntryId); let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(order.id, %entry_id, group, "order traced"); Trail { order_id: order.id, entry_id: entry_id.to_string(), group: group.to_owned(), } } examples/manual/redis_context_stream.rs /// Reads the entry id and the consumer group off the delivery's context. struct Trace; impl Handle<Order, Trail, (), StreamContext> for Trace { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Trail, HandlerOutcome>> { let entry_id = ctx.context(keys::EntryId); let group = ctx.context(keys::ConsumerGroup); tracing::info!(order.id, %entry_id, group, "order traced"); ready(Ok(Trail { order_id: order.id, entry_id: entry_id.to_string(), group: group.to_owned(), })) } }

A stream batch handler's context, StreamBatchContext, carries only the consumer group and the seek handle, which belong to the whole subscription. A batch spans many entries, so a field that differs per entry has no single value for it. The body reads the batch's fields with ctx.context(key): keys::ConsumerGroup, keys::SeekHandle and keys::FredPool. A Ctx<K> parameter binds the per-delivery context, so a batch body reads its fields off the context instead. The handler names the context in its signature, ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamBatchContext>, beside a slice payload. The batch itself is the read's COUNT: .batch(n) at the mount site asks Redis for up to n entries per XREADGROUP.
