Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the stream `orders`; the consumer group comes from the broker. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(place)) } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the stream `orders`; the consumer group comes from the broker. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379").default_group("workers"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(subscriber("orders", Place).build())) }

A slice handler reads one XREADGROUP COUNT on a stream; a list or a channel builds its batch on the client up to the same size. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. The step is required on a slice handler: mounting one without it does not compile. A single-message handler does not offer the step at all; its concurrency is workers(n). On a stream the size is the COUNT of the read that fetches the batch, XREADGROUP or XAUTOCLAIM. The server sends at most n entries, and the handler gets exactly what one read returned, never an empty batch. A list and a channel deliver one value at a time. Their subscriptions gather a batch on the client from the values already waiting, up to the same n, and hand it over without waiting for more. So a batch is often smaller than n, and a quiet key yields batches of one. One outcome settles every entry of the batch. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) settles the batch with an ack and Err(outcomes) settles entry i with outcome i. A stream batch reads a StreamBatchContext, which carries the group and its seek handle and no field of one entry. The block step chains after the size.

Three values waiting on each form arrive in one call. The stream handler and the app: Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Bills the orders one read returned, at most 16. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"))] async fn bill(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(bill.batch(nonzero!(16))) .include(pack.batch(nonzero!(16))) .include(count.batch(nonzero!(16))) }) } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Bills the orders one read returned. struct Bill; impl Handle<[Order]> for Bill { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "orders billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { let broker = RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Bill).batch(nonzero!(16)).build()) .include( subscriber(RedisList::new("jobs"), Pack) .batch(nonzero!(16)) .build(), ) .include( subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("clicks"), Count) .batch(nonzero!(16)) .build(), ) }) } The list and the channel handlers: Macros Manual examples/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Packs the jobs waiting on the list `jobs`, at most 16 at once. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("jobs"))] async fn pack(jobs: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Counts the clicks heard on the channel `clicks`, at most 16 at once. #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("clicks"))] async fn count(clicks: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = clicks.len(), "clicks counted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/redis_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Packs the jobs waiting on the list `jobs`. struct Pack; impl Handle<[Order]> for Pack { fn handle( &self, jobs: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = jobs.len(), "jobs packed"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Counts the clicks heard on the channel `clicks`. struct Count; impl Handle<[Order]> for Count { fn handle( &self, clicks: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = clicks.len(), "clicks counted"); ready(Ok(())) } }

block sets how long one read waits on the server: the XREADGROUP BLOCK on a stream, the BRPOP or BLMOVE timeout on a list. The wait is five seconds unless a subscription names another. A descriptor names it with RedisStream::block or RedisList::block. The mount site names it with the block step, which overrides the descriptor. The step chains after another step of the mount chain: after .batch(n), after .pipeline(), or, in the manual form, after build(). It reads the same before and after start_at(..). On a reclaim subscription the wait is the pause between two XAUTOCLAIM scans that found nothing. A read wakes as soon as an entry arrives, so the wait costs nothing on a busy stream. It decides how soon an idle read sees what happens beside it: a seek of its group, or a due entry of a delay queue, which the subscription sweeps once per read. A shorter wait sees them sooner, at the price of one more round trip per idle wait. The step exists on stream and list subscriptions, the two forms whose read blocks.

Orders wait at most a second per read; invoices are billed sixteen at a time, with a two-second wait set at the mount site. An envelope is how a message's headers travel beside its payload; the broker names one, and a descriptor or a publish policy names its own. A list element and a channel message are one value, and a stream entry is a map of fields. An envelope is the layout of the headers and the payload in them. RedisBroker::envelope sets the broker's envelope, and every subscription and publish policy uses it unless it names its own. A subscription names its own at the mount site with RedisEnvelopeExt::envelope: b.include(handler.envelope(FastStream)). On the manual path the descriptor names it: RedisList::new("jobs").envelope(FastStream). A publish policy names its own with envelope(..): RedisListPublish::new().envelope(FastStream). The envelope is a type, so the choice costs nothing per message. A delivery finds its payload without reading the headers, and reads them the first time a handler asks. A header block that does not parse reads as no headers, and the subscription logs a warning; a handler that requires a header then meets the ordinary missing-header error. Envelope List element, channel message Stream entry envelope::RustStream, the default a binary frame that opens with a marker; a message without headers is its bare payload the payload in _payload, each header in h:<name> FastStream faststream's BinaryMessageFormatV1 the same frame in __data__ Framed a {headers, payload} document written by a codec, its payload in CloudEvents' convention the document in _payload NoOp the payload alone the payload in _payload envelope::RustStream writes the bytes every earlier release wrote, so services on different releases read each other. A binary frame written by 0.7.1 or an earlier release has no marker and reads as its payload, frame bytes included, so services that share a list or a channel upgrade together. FastStream shares lists, channels and streams with a faststream service in both directions. Its header names travel as they are, so faststream's own headers arrive as correlation_id and reply_to. Framed with JsonCodec writes text that redis-cli and RedisInsight show as it is. Its payload follows the convention of CloudEvents' JSON format. A payload that is a JSON text is embedded as the value it is and reads back byte for byte: {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload":{"id":7}}. Any other payload travels as standard base64: {"headers":{"event":"created"},"payload_base64":"CAc="}. With CBOR, msgpack or a codec of the service's own the payload is a byte string in payload; the codec implements FrameCodec, which this crate's json, cbor and msgpack features do for the framework's codecs. A header is a text field, and a header whose value is not text refuses the publish. The document of the codec(..) framing of 0.7.2 and earlier releases carried its payload as a string, so Framed reads it as a JSON string; services that share such a list switch together, and the list is drained first. A value that is not one of the envelope's own arrives as the payload with no headers, whatever its first bytes are. A stream entry without the envelope's field arrives as one JSON object of its fields. A payload that only looks like an envelope is written so that it reads back unchanged. A subscription and the publishers that write its name use one envelope. The broker's default publisher, which writes a retry copy and a reply that name no policy, writes the broker's envelope and the built-in ones. A subscription that reads through an envelope of the service's own, on a broker with another one, has its retry copies published through a policy that names it, out_retry(Publish::new().envelope(MyEnvelope)); the default publisher refuses that name, and the error names it. Two subscriptions that read one name through different envelopes stop the service at startup. NoOp has no room for headers, so a delivery read through it carries none of the message's. The headers a stream read itself reports, the delivery count and the idle time of a claiming read, stay. A publish through it that carries a header fails, and the error names the header and the destination. A retry copy the runtime publishes carries its retry count in a header, so a retry through NoOp fails the same way.

TestApp::start runs the service's app on RedisBroker connected to a Redis modelled in process, groups, lists and channels included. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<RedisBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The connected broker is the production one. Every command it sends, a publish, a group read, an acknowledgement, a delay-queue sweep, reaches the model as that command and is answered as Redis answers it. The model reads every setting off the broker. Its address is parsed as the connect parses it, and the pool size, the default group and the cluster topology carry over. It answers as Redis 8.4, so a claiming subscription mounts. It keeps key types: a write or a read of the wrong type fails with WRONGTYPE. It keeps consumer groups with their cursor, pending entries and delivery counts, the group's start_id, XAUTOCLAIM and XREADGROUP ... CLAIM at their idle thresholds, and a seek. It keeps lists with the processing list and its recovery set, sorted sets, key expiry and MULTI / EXEC. Pub/Sub channels, globs and sharded channels deliver to the subscriptions open at that moment and store nothing for one that is not. On a cluster topology it refuses a command or a transaction that spans hash slots. It runs no scripts: EVAL, EVALSHA, FCALL and a command it does not know fail with an error naming them. No handshake runs, so AUTH, HELLO and TLS are for a live test. A test's input goes where the default publisher writes its name: an XADD, or the LPUSH or PUBLISH of the subscription that reads the name. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply included, so the assertions that follow read finished state. published::<T>(name) reads every write to the name back, a requeued copy and an entry a delay queue adds back included. The model's time is the test's clock: entry ids, idle times and the scores of the delay queue and the recovery set stand still on a paused clock, and tb.advance(by) moves them. A handler's own commands, through FredPool or a pipeline window, reach the model too.

A stream publisher sends a group of publishes as one MULTI and EXEC block; a batch's replies commit together with .transactional(). The stream publisher, RedisPublisher, buffers the publishes of a transaction and sends them on commit, in publish order. Subscribers then see the whole group or none of it. It offers both kinds of transaction the framework defines. A mount that publishes in transactions names RedisTransactionalPublish, TransactionalPublish in the stream prelude, which pairs into the same publisher. This page is the borrowed kind; transaction and owned_transaction are the owned kind. The borrowed kind is the core's TransactionalPublisher: one transaction on the publisher handle. begin_transaction starts buffering, commit flushes the buffer, abort discards it, and a clone of the handle works with the same open transaction. A second begin_transaction while one is open returns RedisError::TransactionBusy and leaves the open one alone. A commit or an abort with nothing open returns RedisError::NoTransaction. Its usual shape is a batch handler whose replies commit together: .transactional() after .out_reply(TransactionalPublish) asks for it, and a policy without transactions does not compile there. Transactions run on standalone and sentinel deployments. A MULTI block cannot span hash slots, so on a cluster TransactionalPublish refuses to pair and the service does not start. The error is RedisError::InvalidOptions, raised before the service reads its first batch. Redis does not roll back: a command that fails inside EXEC leaves the commands before it committed. For a group of XADDs that happens when Redis runs out of memory or a key holds another type. A command the server refuses to queue discards the whole block instead. The list and Pub/Sub publishers send each message on its own.

Each batch's replies reach processed in one block. owned_transaction is the same buffer over values, encoding each one with the default codec. It is the owned kind on a live publisher outside a handler, where no slot carries a codec: the publisher an after_startup hook is handed, for one. publisher.owned_transaction() returns a TypedTransaction that owns its buffer. publish(name, &value) encodes the value and buffers it; commit sends the buffer as one MULTI / EXEC block, and abort discards it. As with transaction, any number can be open on one publisher, and commit and abort consume the value. after_startup runs its hook once the broker is connected and the subscriptions are open, with the policy it names paired into a live publisher. That makes it the place for a service's first publishes, such as seed data that must arrive whole. A hook that returns an error fails the startup. On a cluster TransactionalPublish refuses to pair, so the service does not start and seeds nothing.

The service writes its opening prices as one block once it is connected; the catalog reader sees both or neither. Macros Manual examples/redis_transactions_owned.rs /// Writes the opening prices as one block: readers of `prices` see the whole list or none of it. async fn seed_prices<P: OwnedTransactions>( publisher: P, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let mut seed = publisher.owned_transaction().await?; for (sku, cents) in [("tea", 450), ("cake", 600)] { let price = Price { sku: sku.to_owned(), cents, }; seed.publish("prices", &price).await?; } seed.commit().await?; Ok(()) } /// The service on `broker`: a standalone or a sentinel deployment, where `MULTI` / `EXEC` runs. fn app_on(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("catalog", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Runs once the broker is connected and the subscription is open. b.after_startup(TransactionalPublish, async move |publisher| { seed_prices(publisher).await.map_err(io::Error::other) }) .include(list_price) }) } examples/manual/redis_transactions_owned.rs /// Writes the opening prices as one block: readers of `prices` see the whole list or none of it. async fn seed_prices<P: OwnedTransactions>( publisher: P, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { let mut seed = publisher.owned_transaction().await?; for (sku, cents) in [("tea", 450), ("cake", 600)] { let price = Price { sku: sku.to_owned(), cents, }; seed.publish("prices", &price).await?; } seed.commit().await?; Ok(()) } /// The service on `broker`: a standalone or a sentinel deployment, where `MULTI` / `EXEC` runs. fn app_on(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("catalog", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let list_price = subscriber(RedisStream::new("prices").group("catalog"), ListPrice); // Runs once the broker is connected and the subscription is open. b.after_startup(TransactionalPublish, async move |publisher| { seed_prices(publisher).await.map_err(io::Error::other) }) .include(list_price.build()) }) }

transaction hands back a value that owns its buffer, so several can be open at once and a double commit does not compile. This is the owned kind, the core's OwnedTransactions. A handler takes its slot as Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Slot> and calls transaction() on it. The value it gets back publishes like the slot, txn.message(&value).publish(), and admits the types the slot admits. Each call opens a buffer of its own, so the workers of a workers(n) subscription never share one, and the slot keeps publishing directly meanwhile. commit sends the buffer as one MULTI / EXEC block; abort discards it. Both consume the value, so a second commit or a publish after settling does not compile. Dropping a transaction that was neither committed nor aborted discards its buffer, as an abort does, and writes a warning. A commit that fails has consumed the transaction, and its buffer is gone. The recovery is to redeliver the input, which a retry outcome does, not to send the buffer again. The live transaction is a RedisTransaction, with the same limits as the borrowed kind: standalone and sentinel only, no rollback. The slot's policy is TransactionalPublish, so a cluster refuses it at startup.

An order ships one entry per item in one block, on four workers at once; an item without a name aborts the transaction, which discards the entries already buffered. Macros Manual examples/redis_transactions_transaction.rs /// One shipment per item, committed as one block; four orders ship at once. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("shipping"), workers(4))] async fn ship( order: &Order, Out(shipments): Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(mut txn) = shipments.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an item has no name, the order ships nothing"); // The abort discards the shipments the transaction buffered so far. return match txn.abort().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), }; } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; if txn.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } match txn.commit().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(ship).out(Shipments, TransactionalPublish) }) } examples/manual/redis_transactions_transaction.rs /// One shipment per item, committed as one block; four orders ship at once. struct Ship; impl<S> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(S,)>> for Ship where S: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: OwnedTransactions>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(S,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut txn = outs .get(Shipments) .transaction() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; for item in &order.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(order.id, "an item has no name, the order ships nothing"); // The abort discards the shipments the transaction buffered so far. txn.abort().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: order.id, item: item.clone(), }; txn.message(&shipment) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; } txn.commit().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let ship = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("shipping"), Ship); b.include(ship.workers(nonzero!(4)).build()) .out(Shipments, TransactionalPublish) }, ) }

This guide compares the three Redis structures a service reads: a stream, a list and a Pub/Sub channel. The example is a shop service that uses all three. Orders are billed off a stream, thumbnails are rendered off a list, and price changes arrive on a channel.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "invoices")] struct Invoice { order_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"), reply)] async fn bill(order: &Order) -> Invoice { tracing::info!(order.id, "order billed"); Invoice { order_id: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Invoice { order_id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } named!(Order, "orders"); named!(Invoice, "invoices"); struct Bill; impl Handle<Order, Invoice> for Bill { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Invoice, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order billed"); ready(Ok(Invoice { order_id: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, })) } } A Redis stream keeps every entry until the service trims it. RedisStream reads it through a consumer group. Each group receives every entry once, and inside a group one consumer handles it. An acknowledged entry is XACKed. An entry a consumer never acknowledged stays in the group's pending entries list, so a crash loses nothing. A stream can be read again from an earlier entry with a seek. Orders are money, so they go on a stream. bill answers each order with an Invoice, which lands on the stream invoices.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "thumbnails")] struct Thumbnail { image: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "thumbnails.ready")] struct ThumbnailReady { image: String, } #[subscriber(RedisList::new("thumbnails").reliable(), reply)] async fn render(job: &Thumbnail) -> ThumbnailReady { tracing::info!(job.image, "thumbnail rendered"); ThumbnailReady { image: job.image.clone(), } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Thumbnail { image: String, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct ThumbnailReady { image: String, } named!(Thumbnail, "thumbnails"); named!(ThumbnailReady, "thumbnails.ready"); struct Render; impl Handle<Thumbnail, ThumbnailReady> for Render { fn handle( &self, job: &Thumbnail, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<ThumbnailReady, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.image, "thumbnail rendered"); ready(Ok(ThumbnailReady { image: job.image.clone(), })) } } A Redis list is a queue: a producer pushes an entry, and exactly one consumer pops it. RedisList::new pops with BRPOP, so the entry leaves Redis before the handler runs, and a crash in the handler loses it. reliable moves the entry to a processing list instead and removes it only once the handler acknowledges it. A list has no groups and no replay. Rendering a thumbnail is work for one worker, so the jobs go on a reliable list. render announces each finished thumbnail on the channel thumbnails.ready.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "prices")] struct PriceChange { sku: String, price_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("prices"))] async fn refresh_price(change: &PriceChange) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(change.sku, change.price_cents, "price cache refreshed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct PriceChange { sku: String, price_cents: u64, } named!(PriceChange, "prices"); struct RefreshPrice; impl Handle<PriceChange> for RefreshPrice { fn handle( &self, change: &PriceChange, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(change.sku, change.price_cents, "price cache refreshed"); ready(Ok(())) } } A Pub/Sub message reaches every subscriber connected at the moment it is published. Redis keeps nothing: a subscriber that is not connected never sees the message. RedisPubSub has no acknowledgement, so the outcome a handler returns settles nothing. A price change matters only to the instances running now, which refresh their cache, so it goes on a channel.

Stream List Pub/Sub Kept while nobody reads until trimmed until popped no Who receives a message one consumer in every group one consumer every connected subscriber ack XACK reliable: LREM off the processing list; simple: nothing nothing retry a copy appended to the stream reliable: back to the list; simple: lost lost retry_after a copy after the delay a copy after the delay a copy after the delay A batch one read of up to n entries assembled by the client assembled by the client Replay a seek of the group none none The acknowledgement pages give each outcome in full, and Retries, delays and dead letters shows how a delay and a cap work on each structure. A batch on a stream is the COUNT of one read. A list and a channel deliver one entry at a time, so the client collects a batch of the same size. A name holds one structure. A stream and a list are keys of a type, and a write of the other type fails with WRONGTYPE. A channel is no key at all: an XADD under a channel's name writes a stream its subscribers never see.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(bill) .out_reply(stream::Publish) .include(render) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::default()) .include(refresh_price) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("billing"), Bill) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(stream::Publish) .include( subscriber(RedisList::new("thumbnails").reliable(), Render) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::default()) .include(subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("prices"), RefreshPrice).build()) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } A service on one transport imports that transport's prelude, such as ruststream_fred::stream::prelude. This one mixes transports, so it imports ruststream_fred::prelude. There each transport's publish policy keeps its module's name: stream::Publish writes with XADD, pubsub::Publish with PUBLISH. A reply type names where the reply goes, and the policy at the mount site names how it gets there. The three handlers have the same shape. Moving a handler to another transport changes the descriptor in its attribute and the policy at its mount site, not its body. The tests in the example file publish to each transport and read what the handlers sent back, all in process.

This guide runs a service on a Redis Cluster and names its keys so that the keys a command uses together share a hash slot. The example is a shop backend. It runs jobs off a work queue, invoices orders off a stream, and listens to events on a sharded channel.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(run_job) .include(invoice.pipeline().atomic()) .include(on_event) }) } /// Two seeds: the client reaches the cluster through whichever answers first. #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::cluster([ "redis-1.internal:6379", "redis-2.internal:6379", ])) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let invoice = subscriber(RedisStream::new("{orders}").group("billing"), Invoice); let events = RedisPubSub::new("events").mode(PubSubMode::Sharded); b.include(subscriber(RedisList::new("{jobs}").reliable(), RunJob).build()) .include(invoice.pipeline().atomic().build()) .include(subscriber(events, OnEvent).build()) }) } /// Two seeds: the client reaches the cluster through whichever answers first. fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::cluster([ "redis-1.internal:6379", "redis-2.internal:6379", ])) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } RedisBroker::cluster takes seed nodes. One reachable seed is enough: the client reads the cluster's layout from it and connects to every primary. The constructor does no I/O, like every constructor of the broker; the connection opens when the service starts. The handlers do not change between a standalone server and a cluster. What changes is how the service names its keys.

A cluster splits keys over 16384 hash slots, and each primary owns a range of them. A command, a MULTI block or a script that touches several keys runs only if all of them are on one slot. A hash tag decides the slot: when a key has a part in braces, only that part is hashed. {jobs} and {jobs}.processing share a slot, and so do {orders} and {orders}:invoices. A name in braces cannot be the fixed destination of a type, because #[outgoing(name = "..")] reads braces as a name template. A producer names such a key where it publishes: .message(&job).to("{jobs}").

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The hash tag `{jobs}` keeps the queue and its processing list `{jobs}.processing` on one slot. #[subscriber(RedisList::new("{jobs}").reliable())] async fn run_job(job: &Job) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.id, "job done"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// The hash tag `{jobs}` keeps the queue and its processing list `{jobs}.processing` on one slot. struct RunJob; impl Handle<Job> for RunJob { fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.id, "job done"); ready(Ok(())) } } A reliable list moves each entry to a processing list with one LMOVE, so both keys must be on one slot. The processing list is the queue's name with .processing appended, and it keeps the queue's hash tag. A reliable list whose two keys land on different slots does not start, and the error names the hash tag to use.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Invoices an order; the invoice and the acknowledgement commit as one block on the slot of /// `{orders}`. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("{orders}").group("billing"))] async fn invoice(order: &Order, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>) -> HandlerOutcome { if pipeline .lpush("{orders}:invoices", order.id.to_string()) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Invoices an order; the invoice and the acknowledgement commit as one block on the slot of /// `{orders}`. struct Invoice; impl Handle<Order, (), (), PipelineContext> for Invoice { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { ctx.context(keys::Pipeline) .lpush("{orders}:invoices", order.id.to_string()) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } A stream is one key, so a stream subscription works under any name. An atomic window puts the handler's commands and the XACK in one MULTI block, and the block runs on the stream's slot. invoice writes to {orders}:invoices, on the slot of the stream {orders}. A command for a key on another slot makes Redis refuse the whole block: nothing is written and the entry stays pending. A transaction of the stream publisher is a MULTI block too, and its destinations are not tied to one slot. So a service that mounts TransactionalPublish does not start on a cluster.
documents.s: Side effects on the stream's slot

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Sharded Pub/Sub: the channel lives on the node that owns its slot. #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("events").mode(PubSubMode::Sharded))] async fn on_event(event: &Event) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.kind, "event received"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Sharded Pub/Sub: the channel lives on the node that owns its slot. struct OnEvent; impl Handle<Event> for OnEvent { fn handle( &self, event: &Event, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.kind, "event received"); ready(Ok(())) } } Classic Pub/Sub on a cluster sends every message to every node. PubSubMode::Sharded sends it only to the node that owns the channel's slot, with SPUBLISH and SSUBSCRIBE, so the traffic scales with the cluster. It needs Redis 7 or later. The two modes do not reach each other: a sharded message never reaches a classic subscriber, and the other way round. A publisher of the channel uses the subscription's mode. A pattern subscription is classic only.

The tests start the production app under TestApp::start, with the cluster broker. The in-process Redis behaves like a cluster: it refuses a command or a block that spans hash slots. So the tests check that every form runs with the service's hash tags, that a reliable list without one does not start, and that a block across two slots commits nothing. The same test body runs against a real cluster when REDIS_CLUSTER_TEST_URL names a node. A failover or a resharding happens only on a real cluster; the production guide covers what the broker does then.

This guide shares a Redis stream between workers and between services, and recovers the entries a stopped worker left unfinished. The example is a payments service. Payments arrive on the stream payments. The ledger group posts each payment, and the fraud group screens it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Longer than the slowest posting ever takes: an entry idle this long belongs to no live worker. const MIN_IDLE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber( RedisStream::claiming("payments", MIN_IDLE).group("ledger"), workers(8, by_key) )] async fn post_payment(payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let earlier_deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); if payment.account.starts_with("migrating-") { tracing::warn!( payment.id, earlier_deliveries, "account locked, payment left pending" ); return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, earlier_deliveries, "payment posted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Longer than the slowest posting ever takes: an entry idle this long belongs to no live worker. const MIN_IDLE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { id: u64, account: String, amount_cents: u64, } named!(Payment, "payments"); struct PostPayment; impl Handle<Payment> for PostPayment { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let earlier_deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); if payment.account.starts_with("migrating-") { tracing::warn!( payment.id, earlier_deliveries, "account locked, payment left pending" ); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())); } tracing::info!(payment.id, earlier_deliveries, "payment posted"); ready(Ok(())) } } A Redis stream is read through a consumer group. The group holds a cursor into the stream, and every entry past the cursor goes to one consumer of the group. Each subscription is one consumer, so every running instance of the service adds a consumer to ledger, and the instances share the payments. A consumer gets a generated name, ruststream-0, ruststream-1 and so on in each process. consumer names it, for example after the host, so XINFO CONSUMERS tells the instances apart. An entry handed to a consumer goes into the group's pending entries list. It leaves the list when the handler acknowledges it. If the worker stops first, a crash or a deploy, the entry stays pending: Redis keeps it, and no other consumer receives it on its own. RedisStream::claiming reads both sets in one call: entries pending for at least min_idle, then new ones. So the subscription that takes new payments also takes over the payments of a worker that stopped. It needs Redis 8.4 or later; on an older server the service does not start, and the error names the subscription and both versions. A retry on this subscription does not append a copy. The entry stays pending under its own id, and the next read claims it once it has been idle min_idle. post_payment uses that for an account that is being migrated: the payment waits in the pending list and comes back every 30 seconds. A claimed entry carries DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER: the number of deliveries before this one, zero for a new entry. IDLE_MS_HEADER carries how long the entry sat idle. Retries, delays and dead letters caps the deliveries on this count.

min_idle has no default. An entry idle that long is treated as abandoned, so set it above the longest time a handler ever runs. A shorter value takes an entry away from a worker that is still on it, and the payment is posted twice. A longer value delays recovery after a crash by the same amount.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments.screened")] struct Screened { payment_id: u64, suspicious: bool, } #[subscriber( RedisStream::new("payments") .group("fraud") .start_id(StreamStart::Beginning), reply )] async fn screen_payment(payment: &Payment) -> Screened { Screened { payment_id: payment.id, suspicious: payment.amount_cents > 1_000_000, } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Screened { payment_id: u64, suspicious: bool, } named!(Screened, "payments.screened"); struct ScreenPayment; impl Handle<Payment, Screened> for ScreenPayment { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Screened, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Screened { payment_id: payment.id, suspicious: payment.amount_cents > 1_000_000, })) } } Each group has its own cursor and its own pending list, so each group reads every entry. The fraud group receives every payment the ledger group receives, and neither slows the other. In practice each service that reads a stream has a group of its own. The service creates a group at startup when it does not exist yet. start_id says where a new group starts: StreamStart::New, the default, reads only entries added after that, and StreamStart::Beginning reads every entry the stream still holds. The fraud group was added after the ledger, so it starts at the beginning and screens the payments already on the stream. An existing group keeps its cursor, and start_id does not move it; start_at does.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(post_payment) .include(screen_payment) .out_reply(Publish) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( RedisStream::claiming("payments", MIN_IDLE).group("ledger"), PostPayment, ) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build(), ) .include( subscriber( RedisStream::new("payments") .group("fraud") .start_id(StreamStart::Beginning), ScreenPayment, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } screen_payment replies with a Screened on the stream payments.screened.

workers(8, by_key) runs post_payment on eight lanes. Payments that share a partition key go to the same lane, one after another, so the payments of one account are posted in the order they were added. Redis has no partitions, so the key travels in the PARTITION_KEY_HEADER header. The producer sets it with the partition_key step of its publish. A payment without a key goes to any lane. The order holds inside one consumer; two instances of the service each post their own share of the payments.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("payments").group("ledger"))] async fn post_new_payment(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment posted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(RedisStream::reclaim("payments", MIN_IDLE).group("ledger"))] async fn recover_payment(payment: &Payment, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::warn!( payment.id, deliveries, "payment recovered from a stopped worker" ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app_before_8_4() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(post_new_payment) .include(recover_payment) .include(screen_payment) .out_reply(Publish) }, ) } src/main.rs struct PostNewPayment; impl Handle<Payment> for PostNewPayment { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment posted"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct RecoverPayment; impl Handle<Payment> for RecoverPayment { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let deliveries = ctx.headers().get_str(DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("1"); tracing::warn!( payment.id, deliveries, "payment recovered from a stopped worker" ); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app_before_8_4() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include( subscriber(RedisStream::new("payments").group("ledger"), PostNewPayment).build(), ) .include( subscriber( RedisStream::reclaim("payments", MIN_IDLE).group("ledger"), RecoverPayment, ) .build(), ) .include( subscriber( RedisStream::new("payments") .group("fraud") .start_id(StreamStart::Beginning), ScreenPayment, ) .reply() .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) }, ) } An older server has no claiming read, so recovery is a second subscription on the same group. RedisStream::new reads new entries. RedisStream::reclaim reads only entries pending for at least min_idle, with XAUTOCLAIM, so it takes over what a stopped worker held. A reclaimed delivery counts itself in DELIVERY_COUNT_HEADER, so the first recovery reports at least 1. On a new subscription, retry appends a copy of the entry to the stream and acknowledges the original. The copy comes back at once, behind the entries added meanwhile. A wait such as the migration above takes retry_after there, which Retries, delays and dead letters covers.

The tests in the example file run the service in process on a paused clock. One publishes a payment for an account under migration, moves the clock by min_idle with tb.advance, and sees the ledger receive the payment a second time, with no copy on the stream. Testing a Redis service covers the harness.

This guide broadcasts messages to every running instance of a service with Redis Pub/Sub. The example is a storefront. Every instance refreshes its price cache when a price changes, follows order events through a pattern, and announces shipped orders.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "prices.changed")] struct PriceChanged { sku: String, price_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("prices.changed").buffer(nonzero!(1_000)))] async fn refresh_price(change: &PriceChanged) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(change.sku, change.price_cents, "price cache refreshed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("prices.changed"))] async fn reindex_price(change: &PriceChanged) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(change.sku, "search index updated"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct PriceChanged { sku: String, price_cents: u64, } outgoing!(PriceChanged, "prices.changed"); struct RefreshPrice; impl Handle<PriceChanged> for RefreshPrice { fn handle( &self, change: &PriceChanged, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(change.sku, change.price_cents, "price cache refreshed"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct ReindexPrice; impl Handle<PriceChanged> for ReindexPrice { fn handle( &self, change: &PriceChanged, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(change.sku, "search index updated"); ready(Ok(())) } } RedisPubSub subscribes to one channel. A message published to the channel reaches every subscription connected at that moment: refresh_price and reindex_price both receive it, in every running instance. Nothing is shared out and nothing is acknowledged; the outcome a handler returns settles nothing. Redis keeps no copy. A message published while no subscription is connected is gone, and so is one published to an instance that is restarting. A subscription opens only once Redis has routed its channel to it, so a message published after the service has started is not lost.

Redis pushes each message as soon as it is published, whether the handler is ready or not. The subscription holds what the handler has not taken yet, up to its buffer: 32 messages unless buffer sets another size. Once the buffer is full, each new message drops the oldest, and the subscription logs a warning with the channel and the number it lost. refresh_price sets a buffer of a thousand messages, so a burst of price changes waits for it instead of being cut. The buffer is reserved when the subscription opens, about 600 bytes per message whatever the payloads weigh.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct OrderEvent { order_id: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisPubSubPattern::new("orders.events.*"))] async fn track_order(event: &OrderEvent, Ctx(channel): Ctx<keys::Channel>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order_id, channel, "order event"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderEvent { order_id: u64, } outgoing!(OrderEvent); struct TrackOrder; impl Handle<OrderEvent, (), (), PubSubContext> for TrackOrder { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PubSubContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let channel = ctx.context(keys::Channel); tracing::info!(event.order_id, channel, "order event"); ready(Ok(())) } } RedisPubSubPattern subscribes to a glob with PSUBSCRIBE, here every channel under orders.events.. The handler reads the channel a message came on from the Pub/Sub context with Ctx<keys::Channel>. keys::FromPattern tells whether the message matched through a pattern.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments")] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, } #[subscriber( RedisStream::new("shipments").group("notifier"), reply("orders.events.shipped") )] async fn announce_shipment(shipment: &Shipment) -> OrderEvent { OrderEvent { order_id: shipment.order_id, } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Shipment { order_id: u64, } outgoing!(Shipment, "shipments"); struct AnnounceShipment; impl Handle<Shipment, OrderEvent> for AnnounceShipment { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderEvent, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(OrderEvent { order_id: shipment.order_id, })) } } announce_shipment reads shipments off a stream and replies with an OrderEvent on the channel orders.events.shipped. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("storefront", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(refresh_price) .include(reindex_price) // A glob is no channel a publish can reach, so the registration names one for copies. .include(track_order) .out_retry(pubsub::Publish::default()) .to("orders.events.retry") .include(announce_shipment) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::default()) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("storefront", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( RedisPubSub::new("prices.changed").buffer(nonzero!(1_000)), RefreshPrice, ) .build(), ) .include(subscriber(RedisPubSub::new("prices.changed"), ReindexPrice).build()) // A glob is no channel a publish can reach, so the registration names one for copies. .include(subscriber(RedisPubSubPattern::new("orders.events.*"), TrackOrder).build()) .out_retry(pubsub::Publish::default()) .to("orders.events.retry") .include( subscriber( RedisStream::new("shipments").group("notifier"), AnnounceShipment, ) .reply() .to("orders.events.shipped") .build(), ) .out_reply(pubsub::Publish::default()) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The reply leaves through pubsub::Publish, which sends PUBLISH. The broker's default publisher treats a name that no subscription of this service reads as a stream key and sends XADD to it. The pattern subscription does not read orders.events.shipped by name, so the registration names the Pub/Sub policy. The pattern subscription in the same service receives the announcement. A pattern names no channel a copy could be published to. So track_order's registration names one with out_retry(..).to("orders.events.retry"), and the service does not start without it. That channel matches the pattern, so a retried event comes back to the handler, in every running instance.

On a cluster, a classic PUBLISH goes to every node. PubSubMode::Sharded uses SSUBSCRIBE and SPUBLISH instead: a channel lives on the node that owns its hash slot, so the traffic spreads across the cluster. It needs Redis 7 or later and has no patterns. The two modes do not reach each other, so the subscription and the publish policy name the same mode: RedisPubSub::new(..).mode(PubSubMode::Sharded) and pubsub::Publish::new().mode(PubSubMode::Sharded).

The broker reconnects after a dropped connection, a restart of Redis or a failover, and every Pub/Sub subscription subscribes again. The messages published while it was away are not delivered. A sharded subscription is not restored after a resharding moves its slot to another node.

Pub/Sub suits what is useful only now: a cache to refresh, a live dashboard, a notice to every instance. When each reader must receive every message, including the ones published while it was down, use a stream with one consumer group per reader. Each group reads every entry, and an entry stays in the stream until it is trimmed. The tests in the example file publish a price change and a shipment and check that every subscription received what was published.

documents.t: This guide installs ruststream-fred, starts a local Redis and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.8", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-fred = "0.8" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-fred is the Redis broker, built on the fred client. Its testing feature adds the in-process Redis that tests run on. fred is written in Rust, so the build needs no system library. The broker crate has these features, all off by default: Feature What it gives testing the in-process Redis behind TestApp asyncapi the Redis extension in the generated AsyncAPI document tls-rustls, tls-rustls-ring, tls-native-tls TLS, on rustls with aws-lc-rs, on rustls with ring, or on the system's TLS library sentinel-auth separate credentials for the sentinels credential-provider rotating credentials through a callback

One Redis server is enough to develop against: docker run --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8.4 The server listens on localhost:6379. Redis 8.4 serves every feature of the crate; the claiming read mode needs at least that version. Valkey works the same way: RedisBroker::standalone takes a valkey:// URL, and valkeys:// for TLS.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("orders-svc"))] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(take_order) }) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("orders-svc"), TakeOrder).build()) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the Redis stream orders. It acknowledges an order with an amount and drops one without. RedisBroker::standalone takes the server's URL and only records it. The connection opens when the service starts. A Redis stream is read through a consumer group. RedisStream::new("orders").group("orders-svc") names the stream and the group, and the service creates both at startup when they do not exist yet. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Add an order to the stream from another terminal: docker exec redis redis-cli XADD orders '*' _payload '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' The payload goes in the entry's _payload field. The service logs order taken with the order's id. A new group starts at the end of the stream, so the service reads the orders added after its first start. Ctrl+C stops it. cargo generate scaffolds the same kind of service with a router and a reply. There is one template per Redis structure: redis-stream, redis-list and redis-pubsub. cargo generate --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream-fred templates/redis-stream --name my-service

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. RedisBroker connects to an in-process Redis there, so the tests need no server: cargo test Testing a Redis service walks through the tests of a larger service and what the in-process Redis models.

A service on fred writes its own read loop, its acknowledgements and its group setup. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: fred RustStream Builder::from_config(..) and a Pool RedisBroker::standalone, cluster or sentinel, with pool for its size; from_pool takes a pool you built XGROUP CREATE .. MKSTREAM done by the subscription at startup an XREADGROUP loop a #[subscriber] handler on RedisStream decoding the entry's fields the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec XACK after the work the handler's outcome an XAUTOCLAIM loop RedisStream::claiming or reclaim (Consumer groups and crash recovery) a BLMOVE worker with LREM RedisList::reliable (Work queues on lists) a SubscriberClient and its message stream RedisPubSub (Fan-out with Pub/Sub) XADD, LPUSH, PUBLISH a reply or an Out parameter, sent through a publish policy MULTI / EXEC around a group of XADDs a transaction

This guide shows what a RustStream service reads and writes in Redis, so that producers and consumers in other languages share its streams, lists and channels. The example is an order service. A shop written in another language appends orders to a stream, and a mailer written in another language pops emails off a list.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// An order as the shop's producer appends it: `XADD orders * _payload '{"id":1,...}'`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, email: String, } /// An email for the mailer, a worker written in another language. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "emails")] struct Email { to: String, subject: String, } #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("mail"), reply)] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> Email { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); Email { to: order.email.clone(), subject: format!("Order {} received", order.id), } } src/main.rs /// An order as the shop's producer appends it: `XADD orders * _payload '{"id":1,...}'`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, email: String, } /// An email for the mailer, a worker written in another language. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[outgoing(name = "emails")] struct Email { to: String, subject: String, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order, Email> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Email, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order taken"); ready(Ok(Email { to: order.email.clone(), subject: format!("Order {} received", order.id), })) } } A Redis stream entry is a set of fields. A RustStream service keeps the message body in the field _payload and each header in a field named h: followed by the header's name. A producer in any language writes an order the service reads like this: redis-cli XADD orders '*' _payload '{"id":1,"email":"ann@example.com"}' h:trace-id 4bf92f35 The body is what the codec decodes: JSON with the default codec, so the producer writes the order as JSON. A header field is optional; an entry with _payload alone arrives with no headers. Fields with other names are ignored, so a producer can add its own. An entry without _payload is one another program wrote, and its fields become the body as one JSON object. Each value is a string when it is valid UTF-8 and an array of numbers otherwise; the h: fields stay headers: redis-cli XADD orders '*' id 1 email ann@example.com # the body: {"email":"ann@example.com","id":"1"} A consumer in another language reads entries the service writes the same way: _payload holds the body, and the h: fields hold the headers.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379")) } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The envelope in JSON: a value the mailer reads with any JSON parser. b.include(take_order) .out_reply(list::Publish::default().envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec))) }) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379")) } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("mail"); // The envelope in JSON: a value the mailer reads with any JSON parser. b.include(subscriber(orders, TakeOrder).reply().build()) .out_reply(list::Publish::default().envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec))) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } A list entry and a Pub/Sub message are one value, so the headers travel in a frame around the body. A message without headers is written as the bare body. By default the frame is binary, and it opens with a marker header named ruststream-frame with an empty value: Bytes Meaning 4 the number of headers plus one for the marker, a big-endian u32 4, ruststream-frame, 4 the marker: the name's length 16, the name, and the value's length 0 4, then the name for each header: the name's length and the name 4, then the value the value's length and the value the rest the body A body without headers that carries the marker at the place a frame carries it is written in a frame, so it reads back unchanged. An envelope named on the publish policy writes another layout. Framed with JsonCodec writes a JSON document, and the mailer pops a JSON object: redis-cli RPOP emails # {"headers":{},"payload":{"to":"ann@example.com","subject":"Order 1 received"}} payload is the body, here the email embedded as the JSON value it is, so one parse reads the whole document. A body that is not a JSON text travels as base64 in payload_base64 instead, the convention of CloudEvents' JSON format, and a header is a string. The same document shows readable values in a tool like RedisInsight.

A subscription reads the envelope its publisher writes: the mount site names it with RedisEnvelopeExt::envelope, as b.include(handler.envelope(Framed::new(JsonCodec))), and without one the subscription reads the broker's. The JSON document is read only in its exact shape: an object with headers and payload and no other field. A value that is not the envelope's own, such as one another client pushes or publishes as plain JSON, arrives as the body with no headers, whatever its first bytes are: redis-cli LPUSH jobs '{"id":7}' redis-cli PUBLISH prices '{"sku":"tea","cents":450}' So a producer in another language writes plain values unless it needs headers, and then it writes the JSON document. A binary frame written by 0.7.1 or an earlier release has no marker, so a current subscription reads it as the body, frame bytes included. All services that share a list or a channel upgrade together, and a list is drained of the old values first. A subscription of an earlier release reads the new frame, and sees the marker as one more header.

documents.t: A broker built with envelope(FastStream) reads and writes faststream's BinaryMessageFormatV1, the frame a faststream service writes to Redis: Bytes Meaning 8 the identity header \x89BIN\r\n\x1a\n 2 the version, 1 4, 4 where the header block starts and where the body starts, big-endian u32s 2 at the header block: the number of headers, a big-endian u16 2, then the name; 2, then the value for each header: the name's length and the name, the value's length and the value the rest at the body's start: the body A list element and a channel message are the frame, and a stream entry holds it in the field __data__. Every message is framed, headers or none, as faststream frames it. The header names travel as they are: faststream's own headers arrive as correlation_id and reply_to, and a header this service sets reaches a faststream handler under the name it was given. A value without the identity header arrives as the body with no headers.

The test in the example files runs in process: the order arrives as the shop writes it, and the value on emails is the JSON document, byte for byte. A live test reads both from a server with a second fred client, as another program would: the newest entry of orders holds the order under _payload, and the newest value of emails is the document.

This guide sends a handler's own Redis writes together with the acknowledgement of its delivery. The example is an order service. It puts the lines of each order on the warehouse's pick queue, answers with a numbered receipt, and books payments in a ledger.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Puts every line of an order on the warehouse's pick queue and answers with a numbered receipt. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("fulfilment"), reply)] async fn accept( order: &Order, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>, Ctx(pool): Ctx<keys::FredPool>, ) -> Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome> { for line in &order.lines { if line.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, line.sku, "an empty line drops the order"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if pipeline.lpush("picks", line.sku.as_str()).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } // The receipt needs its number now, so the `INCR` goes over the pool, not into the round. let number = pool .incr::<i64, _>("receipts:sequence") .await .map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the receipt sequence is out of reach"); HandlerOutcome::retry() })?; Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id, number, }) } src/main.rs /// Puts every line of an order on the warehouse's pick queue and answers with a numbered receipt. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order, Receipt, (), PipelineContext> for Accept { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome> { let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); for line in &order.lines { if line.quantity == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, line.sku, "an empty line drops the order"); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } if pipeline.lpush("picks", line.sku.as_str()).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } } // The receipt needs its number now, so the `INCR` goes over the pool, not into the round. let number = ctx .context(keys::FredPool) .incr::<i64, _>("receipts:sequence") .await .map_err(|err| { tracing::warn!(order.id, %err, "the receipt sequence is out of reach"); HandlerOutcome::retry() })?; Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id, number, }) } } A handler that writes to Redis and then acknowledges pays two round trips. A crash between them applies the write without the acknowledgement, and the entry is delivered again. Ctx<keys::Pipeline> gives the handler the delivery's round, a RedisPipeline. Its command methods are those of fred: lpush, hincrby, xadd, publish, eval and the rest. A call queues the command and returns at once. Ok means the command is queued, not that Redis has run it. The queued commands leave after the handler returns, and only if it acknowledges the delivery. They go first, then the XACK, in one pipeline. Outcome The queued commands The settle ack sent, before the settle XACK drop discarded XACK retry, retry_after discarded the retry copy, then XACK unsettled discarded none: the entry stays pending accept queues one push per line. A line without a quantity drops the order, and the pushes queued for the earlier lines are discarded with it.

A queued command has no answer inside the handler. A value the handler needs now goes over the broker's connection pool, which Ctx<keys::FredPool> gives. accept numbers each receipt with INCR this way. Beside keys::Pipeline, keys::FredPool comes second in the signature.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // The receipt joins the delivery's round and leaves after the picks. b.include(accept.pipeline()) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(InRound) .include(capture.pipeline().atomic()) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { let accept = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("fulfilment"), Accept); let capture = subscriber(RedisStream::new("{payments}").group("ledger"), Capture); // The receipt joins the delivery's round and leaves after the picks. b.include(accept.pipeline().reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(InRound) .include(capture.pipeline().atomic().build()) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } .pipeline() at the mount site opens the window, and the handler's commands can only be queued on a subscription mounted with it. A handler that takes Ctx<keys::Pipeline> and is mounted without the step does not compile. Without the InRound transform, a reply is published as soon as the handler returns, ahead of the round. The transform on the reply puts it into the round, after the commands, so the receipt leaves only with the picks. A publish through an Out slot joins the round when the handler binds the slot with pipeline.bind(out). The window collects the rounds of every delivery of one read. It leaves when the read's deliveries are all settled, so under load one round trip carries a whole fetched batch. On a trickle it leaves as soon as the last handler returns. A failed flush is reported once, with the subscription and the number of commands and settles it carried. The entries whose XACK failed stay pending and are delivered again. A batch handler takes the round from its context, ctx.context(keys::Pipeline), and its commands leave only if every entry of the batch is acknowledged (Flush).

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Books a payment: the ledger entry, the balance and the acknowledgement commit as one block. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("{payments}").group("ledger"))] async fn capture(payment: &Payment, Ctx(pipeline): Ctx<keys::Pipeline>) -> HandlerOutcome { let entry = format!("{}:{}", payment.id, payment.amount_cents); if pipeline.lpush("{payments}:ledger", entry).await.is_err() || pipeline .hincrby( "{payments}:balances", payment.account.as_str(), payment.amount_cents, ) .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Books a payment: the ledger entry, the balance and the acknowledgement commit as one block. struct Capture; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), PipelineContext> for Capture { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, PipelineContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pipeline = ctx.context(keys::Pipeline); let entry = format!("{}:{}", payment.id, payment.amount_cents); if pipeline.lpush("{payments}:ledger", entry).await.is_err() || pipeline .hincrby( "{payments}:balances", payment.account.as_str(), payment.amount_cents, ) .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } A pipeline is not a transaction: a command can succeed while the XACK after it fails. .atomic() after .pipeline() wraps each delivery's commands and its settle in MULTI and EXEC. The ledger entry, the balance and the acknowledgement of a payment then happen together or not at all. Redis has no rollback. A command that fails inside EXEC, such as an HINCRBY on a key of another type, leaves the others applied. On a cluster a MULTI block runs on one hash slot. The stream is {payments} and the handler's keys are {payments}:ledger and {payments}:balances: the hash tag in braces puts them all on the stream's slot. The stream's name has braces, so the payment type declares no destination and a producer names the stream when it publishes.

eval and evalsha queue a Lua script like any other command, and the script runs in the round with the settle. A script runs atomically on the server, so it suits a check and a write that must not be split. The in-process Redis runs no scripts, so a test of a handler that queues one runs against a server.

The tests in the example files publish an order, a dropped order and a payment in process. They read back the picks, the receipt and the ledger entry, and check that a dropped order sends none of what it queued.
A managed Redis asks a service for an ACL user and TLS, and production asks it to survive a restart of the server. This guide configures the broker for both.

src/main.rs /// Where Redis is and who the service is, as the deployment provides them. struct Deployment { url: String, username: String, password: String, } impl Deployment { fn from_env() -> Self { let read = |name: &str| env::var(name).unwrap_or_default(); Self { url: read("REDIS_URL"), username: read("REDIS_USERNAME"), password: read("REDIS_PASSWORD"), } } } fn broker(deployment: Deployment) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::standalone(deployment.url) .credentials(deployment.username, deployment.password) .pool(8) } The deployment provides the address and the credentials in environment variables, so no secret sits in the source. credentials sets an ACL user and its password, and it works on every topology. It is the only way to authenticate a cluster or a sentinel set, whose seed lists carry no password. On a standalone server it wins over a user and a password written into the URL. password is the older AUTH with a password and no user, for a server configured with requirepass alone.
