documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("orders-svc"), reply)] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { order_id: order.id } } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(confirm).out_reply(Publish)) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker(Deployment::from_env())) } src/main.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { order_id: order.id })) } } fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let orders = RedisStream::new("orders").group("orders-svc"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Confirm).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish) }) } fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { service(broker(Deployment::from_env())) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The handlers do not know how the broker authenticates. The tests start the same service with test credentials under TestApp::start; the in-process Redis checks no password, so the live tests log in to a server with an ACL user.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["tls-rustls"] } TLS is one of three features, mapped onto the TLS backends of fred: tls-rustls (rustls on aws-lc-rs), tls-rustls-ring (rustls on ring) and tls-native-tls (the platform's TLS library). With one of them on, a standalone URL that starts with rediss:// or valkeys:// connects over TLS. tls takes a TlsConnector on any topology, which is how a cluster or a sentinel set gets TLS, and how a service sets its own trust roots or a client certificate. TlsConnector::default_rustls() uses the system's trust roots.

Managed Redis often issues short-lived passwords, such as an IAM token on ElastiCache. The credential-provider feature adds credential_provider: a callback that returns the user and the password for each AUTH or HELLO. It can also log in again at an interval, before the token expires. It wins over static credentials.

src/main.rs /// The primary `orders` as two sentinels report it, with the ACL user the deployment provides. fn sentinel_broker(username: String, password: String) -> RedisBroker { RedisBroker::sentinel( "orders", ["sentinel-1.internal:26379", "sentinel-2.internal:26379"], ) .credentials(username, password) .pool(8) } RedisBroker::sentinel names the primary the sentinels monitor and the sentinels themselves. The client asks the sentinels where the primary is, and asks again after a failover. credentials authenticates to the data nodes. Sentinels with a password of their own take sentinel_credentials, from the sentinel-auth feature.

The broker keeps a pool of connections for publishes, acknowledgements and the commands handlers send. Its size is 4 unless pool(n) sets another, and broker above sets 8. Every stream and list subscription reads on a connection of its own, and every Pub/Sub subscription listens on one, so a blocking read never holds up a publish. A service therefore opens the pool plus one connection per subscription; size the server's client limit for that. Raise the pool size when publishes and acknowledgements queue behind each other under load. A subscription mounted with .pipeline() settles a whole fetched batch in one round trip, which takes load off the pool.

Every connection the broker opens reconnects after the server drops it, as on a restart or a failover. The first attempt follows after 100 ms, each next one waits twice as long, up to 10 s between attempts, with no limit on their number. A command issued meanwhile waits for the connection. What a subscription does once its connection is back: A stream subscription reads on. If the server lost the consumer group, as on a restart that kept no data, the subscription creates the group again and reads the stream from its start. A Pub/Sub subscription subscribes again. Messages published while it was disconnected are lost, as Pub/Sub never keeps them. A sharded Pub/Sub subscription on a cluster is not restored after a resharding moves its channel's slot to another node. The server ends that subscription without dropping the connection, so nothing reconnects; restart the service after a resharding. For another reconnection policy, or any other setting the builders do not reach, build a fred Pool yourself and wrap it with from_pool. The subscriptions' own connections then reconnect by that pool's policy.

The service stops on SIGINT or SIGTERM. The runtime stops reading, lets the handlers settle what they hold, and shuts the broker down: every blocked read ends at once and every connection closes. An entry a stream handler did not get to acknowledge stays pending, and a reclaim or claiming subscription picks it up after a restart.
The AsyncAPI document names the host and port of the server, never the credentials. A broker built with from_pool reports no host, because the pool hides it.

This guide moves a consumer group's cursor on a Redis stream: back to replay entries, forward to skip them. The example is a payments service. It rebuilds a view of balances from the ledger stream, and sends alerts to customers from another stream.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Rebuilds the balance view from the oldest entry the stream retains, on every start. #[subscriber( RedisStream::new("ledger").group("balances"), start_at(RedisGroupPosition::beginning()) )] async fn rebuild(entry: &LedgerEntry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!( entry.seq, entry.account, entry.amount_cents, "balance updated" ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Rebuilds the balance view from the oldest entry the stream retains, on every start. struct Rebuild; impl Handle<LedgerEntry> for Rebuild { fn handle( &self, entry: &LedgerEntry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!( entry.seq, entry.account, entry.amount_cents, "balance updated" ); ready(Ok(())) } } A Redis stream keeps its entries after they are read and acknowledged. A consumer group keeps one cursor over them: the id of the last entry it was given. Replaying means moving that cursor back, which by hand is XGROUP SETID. start_at moves the cursor before the subscription's first delivery, on every start. RedisGroupPosition::beginning is the oldest entry the stream still retains, so rebuild reads the whole ledger each time the service starts. A view rebuilt this way starts from an empty state, such as one held in memory. The cursor belongs to the group, not to the subscription. Every consumer of balances replays, in this service and in every other instance of it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(rebuild).include(notify)) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let ledger = RedisStream::new("ledger").group("balances"); let alerts = RedisStream::new("alerts").group("notifier"); b.include( subscriber(ledger, Rebuild) .build() .start_at(RedisGroupPosition::beginning()), ) .include(subscriber(alerts, Notify).build()) }) } With the macros, start_at(..) is a clause of #[subscriber]. In the manual form it is a step of the mount, after build(). Position Where the group resumes RedisGroupPosition::beginning() the oldest entry the stream retains RedisGroupPosition::end() the tail: only entries added afterwards RedisGroupPosition::after(id) the entry after id, which itself is skipped StreamStart is a different setting: it says where a group starts when it does not exist yet. start_at moves a group that exists, on every start.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Sends alerts. On a halt marker the group moves to the tail, so the alerts queued behind the /// marker are never sent, by this consumer or any other of `notifier`. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("alerts").group("notifier"))] async fn notify(alert: &Alert, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<keys::SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { if !alert.halt { tracing::info!(alert.id, "alert sent"); return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::warn!( group = seeker.group(), "halt marker, the backlog is skipped" ); match seeker.seek(RedisGroupPosition::end()).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } src/main.rs /// Sends alerts. On a halt marker the group moves to the tail, so the alerts queued behind the /// marker are never sent, by this consumer or any other of `notifier`. struct Notify; impl Handle<Alert, (), (), StreamContext> for Notify { async fn handle( &self, alert: &Alert, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, StreamContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if !alert.halt { tracing::info!(alert.id, "alert sent"); return Ok(()); } let seeker = ctx.context(keys::SeekHandle); tracing::warn!( group = seeker.group(), "halt marker, the backlog is skipped" ); seeker .seek(RedisGroupPosition::end()) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } A handler moves its group while the service runs through the seek handle. Ctx<keys::SeekHandle> gives it; its group() names the group it moves. A producer floods the alerts stream by mistake, and an operator appends a halt marker while the flood goes on. notify reads the marker and moves the group to the tail, so the alerts that follow the marker in the stream are never sent. The seek takes effect as soon as it returns. Entries the old cursor had already selected are discarded, not delivered, and a subscription blocked in XREADGROUP reads under the new cursor within one block interval. A batch handler reads the same handle with ctx.context(keys::SeekHandle) on its batch context.

A delivery knows its own position: Ctx<keys::Position> is the cursor that redelivers it. A seek to it delivers the same entry again, then the entries after it, in stream order. A handler that must keep order on a transient failure can seek there instead of returning retry, because on a stream retry appends a copy at the tail. Ctx<keys::EntryId> is the entry's own id, and RedisGroupPosition::after(id) builds a position from an id stored elsewhere.

A seek moves the cursor and nothing else. An entry delivered and not acknowledged stays in the group's pending entries list, and a reclaim or claiming subscription still finds it. A copy waiting in a delay set is appended when it falls due, wherever the group reads. A replayed entry is read as a new delivery, and Redis counts its deliveries from one again. A claiming subscription caps its attempts from the replay on, and the framework's own retry count does not move.

Redis keeps a stream's entries until something trims them, and a replay can only reach what is kept. Trimming with XTRIM is the service's decision: a handler sends it through Ctx<keys::FredPool>, or an operator runs it. A group whose cursor points before the oldest retained entry reads from the oldest one.

The tests in the example files run in process. They check that the view reads every entry and that a halt marker skips the alerts queued behind it. A replay across a restart needs a server that keeps the stream between two starts, so that test runs live, against REDIS_TEST_URL.

This guide retries a message now or later, caps the attempts and moves what keeps failing to a dead-letter stream. Redis has no per-message delay, no dead-letter structure, and a delivery count only inside a stream's consumer group. The framework supplies the rest: the mount site declares the cap and the destination, and the subscription chooses how a delay is kept. The example is a refunds service that sends refunds through a card processor.

The processor refuses a refund in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means its rate limit is used up: a retry right now would be refused again, so retry_after waits 30 seconds. Unavailable means it did not answer: retry tries again at once. Declined means the card account is closed, and another try gets the same answer, so the refund is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber( RedisStream::new("refunds") .group("refunds") .delayed_retry(DelayedRetry::DurableZset { key: "refunds.delayed".to_owned(), ttl: None, }) )] async fn process_refund( refund: &Refund, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { settle(&processor, refund).await } async fn settle(processor: &Processor, refund: &Refund) -> HandlerOutcome { match processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy processor asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Refund { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Refund { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct ProcessRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for ProcessRefund { async fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { settle(&ctx.state().processor, refund).await } } async fn settle(processor: &Processor, refund: &Refund) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match processor.refund(refund).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // Past the rate limit: a delivery right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, "card declined, refund dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } fn refunds() -> RedisStream { RedisStream::new("refunds") .group("refunds") .delayed_retry(DelayedRetry::DurableZset { key: "refunds.delayed".to_owned(), ttl: None, }) } retry on a stream appends a copy of the entry to the stream and acknowledges the original. On the other structures it does what the structure allows: Subscription retry without a cap RedisStream::new, reclaim a copy appended to the stream RedisStream::claiming the entry stays pending and comes back after min_idle RedisList::reliable the entry moves back to the list RedisList::new, RedisPubSub nothing: the message is gone Under a declared cap, retry becomes a copy on every subscription but a claiming one, so the count travels with the message; a claiming entry carries Redis's own count.

retry_after settles the delivery and asks for it again after the delay. A subscription keeps that delay in one of three ways. The framework's own way needs nothing on the descriptor. The runtime holds a copy and publishes it back to the stream key once the delay is up. The copy carries the retry-count header, RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, raised by one. It lives in the process, so a service that stops before the delay ends loses it. DelayedRetry::DurableZset keeps the delay in Redis, which is what process_refund does. A delayed delivery goes into the sorted set refunds.delayed under its due time, with the retry count raised, and the original is acknowledged. As the subscription reads, it moves every due entry back onto the stream under a new id. The delay survives a restart of the service. A sweep runs once per read, so a delay ends within one block interval of its due time, five seconds by default. The scores are wall-clock milliseconds, so the clocks of the service's hosts need to agree. A ttl expires an abandoned set and has to be longer than the longest delay, or entries are lost before they are due. A claiming subscription is the third way, and it needs no set. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(RedisStream::claiming("refunds.priority", BACKOFF).group("refunds"))] async fn process_priority_refund( refund: &Refund, State(processor): State<Arc<Processor>>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { settle(&processor, refund).await } src/main.rs fn priority_refunds() -> RedisStream { RedisStream::claiming("refunds.priority", BACKOFF).group("refunds") } A retry leaves the entry in the group's pending list, and the subscription's own next read takes it back once it has been idle min_idle. Nothing is copied, and the entry keeps its id. The only wait this offers is min_idle, so a shorter delay rounds up to it and a longer one is cut down to it. process_priority_refund sets min_idle to the backoff for that reason. A claiming subscription that names a DurableZset keeps each delay as asked instead.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter stream. b.include(process_refund) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq") .include(process_priority_refund) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq") .include(review) }) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one refund, the first included; then the dead-letter stream. b.include(subscriber(refunds(), ProcessRefund).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq") .include(subscriber(priority_refunds(), ProcessRefund).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("refunds.dlq") .include( subscriber( RedisStream::new("refunds.dlq").group("refunds-review"), Review, ) .build(), ) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } max_attempts counts every delivery of one refund, the first included. The fifth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to refunds.dlq, payload and headers as they arrived. The dead letter is written the way the refund came in, so a refund from a stream lands on the stream refunds.dlq. A cap without a destination rejects the delivery at the cap, and a destination without a cap takes every retry on the first one. A dropped refund settles and goes nowhere; refunds.dlq holds only the refunds that ran out of attempts. The cap reads one count, and where it comes from depends on the subscription. A claiming subscription reads the delivery count Redis keeps for the entry. That count includes the deliveries of a worker that stopped, so a refund that crashed a worker counts against the cap too. Every other subscription reads the retry-count header on the copies the runtime publishes, and the delay set raises it on every round as well. A seek that replays entries delivers them again, as new deliveries. Redis counts a replayed entry's deliveries from one again, so a claiming subscription caps it from the replay on; the retry-count header does not move.
documents.s: The cap and the dead-letter stream

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("refunds.dlq").group("refunds-review"))] async fn review(refund: &Refund, ctx: &mut Context<'_>) -> HandlerOutcome { let retry_count = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); tracing::error!( refund.id, retry_count, "refund needs a person to look at it" ); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Review; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for Review { fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let retry_count = ctx.headers().get_str(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER).unwrap_or("0"); tracing::error!( refund.id, retry_count, "refund needs a person to look at it" ); ready(Ok(())) } } refunds.dlq is an ordinary stream, and review reads it through a group of its own. A refund that came through copies carries the retry-count header, 5 here. review logs the refund for a person to look at.

A copy goes to the address the subscription reports: the stream key, the list key or the channel. A Pub/Sub pattern reads every channel its glob matches and names no single channel. Its registration names where a copy goes with out_retry, as .out_retry(Publish::default()).to("events.retry"), and the service does not start without it.

The tests in the example file run the service in process on a paused clock. tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once, for the delay set and for the claiming subscription alike. Testing a Redis service covers the harness.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process Redis or against a server. The service under test charges card payments. A payment arrives on the stream card-payments, and the handler replies with a receipt on card-receipts. A payment without an amount is dropped. Each account may spend 1,000.00 a day: the handler adds the amount to the key spent:<account> through the broker's connection pool, and holds a payment over the limit for a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a payment goes to card-payments.review, the dead-letter stream. A refund arrives on the reliable list card-refunds and gives the amount back. The app is built by service(url), so a test chooses the server and main uses the production one. The handler calls the pool through fred's command traits, so the service lists fred among its dependencies. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-fred and a Tokio runtime: Cargo.toml [dev-dependencies] ruststream-fred = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt", "rt-multi-thread"] }

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn a_payment_is_answered_with_a_receipt( tb: TestApp<()>, account: &str, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .message(&payment(1, account, 2500)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment_id: 1 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { a_payment_is_answered_with_a_receipt(TestApp::start(app()).await?, "acct-1").await } src/main.rs /// The body both modes run; only the start call differs. async fn a_payment_is_answered_with_a_receipt( tb: TestApp<()>, account: &str, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .message(&payment(1, account, 2500)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment_id: 1 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } #[tokio::test] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { a_payment_is_answered_with_a_receipt(TestApp::start(app()).await?, "acct-1").await } TestApp::start connects RedisBroker to a Redis modelled inside the test process. The URL is never dialled. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<RedisBroker>(). A test's message is written to its name the way the subscription reading that name expects it: LPUSH for a list, PUBLISH for a channel or a pattern, XADD for a stream or a name no subscription reads. publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled, and what reached card-receipts. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .message(&payment(2, "acct-2", 0)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_an_amount_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .message(&payment(2, "acct-2", 0)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } settled checks the outcome the handler returned. assert_not_called checks that no receipt was published.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_held_payment_passes_once_a_refund_frees_room() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let redis = tb.broker::<RedisBroker>(); redis .message(&payment(3, "acct-3", 80_000)) .publish() .await?; redis .message(&payment(4, "acct-3", 30_000)) .publish() .await?; redis .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called(2) .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The refund is a list entry; the handler gives the room back through the pool. redis .message(&Refund { account: "acct-3".to_owned(), amount_cents: 50_000, }) .publish() .await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( redis.subscriber("card-payments").outcomes(), [Outcome::Ack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Ack], ); redis .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called(2) .with(&Receipt { payment_id: 4 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_held_payment_passes_once_a_refund_frees_room() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; let redis = tb.broker::<RedisBroker>(); redis .message(&payment(3, "acct-3", 80_000)) .publish() .await?; redis .message(&payment(4, "acct-3", 30_000)) .publish() .await?; redis .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called(2) .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The refund is a list entry; the handler gives the room back through the pool. redis .message(&Refund { account: "acct-3".to_owned(), amount_cents: 50_000, }) .publish() .await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( redis.subscriber("card-payments").outcomes(), [Outcome::Ack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Ack], ); redis .published::<Receipt>("card-receipts") .assert_called(2) .with(&Receipt { payment_id: 4 }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } The handler's INCRBY and DECRBY run against the in-process Redis, as every command of the crate does. The second payment takes the account over its limit, so it is held. The refund is a list entry, and its handler gives the room back. The test starts on a paused clock, and advance moves it forward. A minute of HOLD costs nothing. The in-process Redis reads the test's clock too, so entry ids, idle times and the scores of a delay set stand still until the clock moves. outcomes lists how each delivery settled, in order; the held one is recorded as Outcome::Nack.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_held_three_times_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .message(&payment(5, "acct-5", 150_000)) .publish() .await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called(3); tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&payment(5, "acct-5", 150_000)) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "3"); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_held_three_times_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(app()).await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .message(&payment(5, "acct-5", 150_000)) .publish() .await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .subscriber("card-payments") .assert_called(3); tb.broker::<RedisBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card-payments.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&payment(5, "acct-5", 150_000)) .with_header(RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, "3"); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } A payment above the daily limit is held on every delivery. Each hold publishes a copy back to the stream with the retry count raised, and published reads every write to a name back, those copies included. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so the payment goes to card-payments.review as it arrived.

The in-process Redis takes the commands the crate sends and answers them as Redis 8.4 does, so a claiming subscription mounts. It reads every setting off the broker: the URL, the pool size, the default group and a cluster topology. It keeps: key types, so a write of the wrong type fails with WRONGTYPE; consumer groups with their cursor, pending entries and delivery counts, XAUTOCLAIM, XREADGROUP .. CLAIM and a seek; lists, with a reliable list's processing list and its recovery set; Pub/Sub channels, patterns and sharded channels, which keep nothing for a subscriber that is not there; sorted sets, key expiry and MULTI / EXEC; on a cluster topology, the refusal of a command or a transaction that spans hash slots. A handler's own commands, through the pool or a pipelined round, run against it too. It runs no scripts: EVAL, EVALSHA, FCALL and a command it does not know fail with an error naming them. No handshake runs, so authentication and TLS are not exercised, and neither is a failover or a resharding. Those need a server.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("REDIS_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; // A server keeps what earlier runs left, so each run spends from an account of its own. let run = SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)?.as_nanos(); let account = format!("acct-{run}"); a_payment_is_answered_with_a_receipt(TestApp::start_live(service(&url)).await?, &account) .await } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn against_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("REDIS_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; // A server keeps what earlier runs left, so each run spends from an account of its own. let run = SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)?.as_nanos(); let account = format!("acct-{run}"); a_payment_is_answered_with_a_receipt(TestApp::start_live(service(&url)).await?, &account) .await } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to a running Redis. A publish then waits on the real clock until every subscription has handled it, ten seconds at most. The test reads the address from REDIS_TEST_URL with live::url, a helper of the example's own, and skips when it is unset. A server keeps what earlier runs left, so the test spends from an account of its own. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. cargo test docker run --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8.4 REDIS_TEST_URL=redis://localhost:6379 cargo test -- --test-threads=1

documents.t: This guide publishes groups of messages to Redis streams all or nothing. The example is an order service. It confirms orders in batches and ships each packed parcel as one shipment per item.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Confirms a batch of orders. The confirmations of one batch are published together or not at /// all. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("confirmations"), reply)] async fn confirm(orders: &[Order]) -> Result<Vec<Confirmation>, HandlerOutcome> { if orders.iter().any(|order| order.items.is_empty()) { tracing::warn!( orders = orders.len(), "a batch with an empty order is dropped" ); return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmation { order_id: order.id }) .collect()) } src/main.rs /// Confirms a batch of orders. The confirmations of one batch are published together or not at /// all. struct Confirm; impl Handle<[Order], Vec<Confirmation>> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<Confirmation>, Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { if orders.iter().any(|order| order.items.is_empty()) { tracing::warn!( orders = orders.len(), "a batch with an empty order is dropped" ); return ready(Err(orders.iter().map(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop()).collect())); } ready(Ok(orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmation { order_id: order.id }) .collect())) } } A transaction sends its publishes as one MULTI and EXEC block, in publish order. A reader of confirmations sees every confirmation of a batch, or none of them. confirm is a batch handler: it takes a slice and returns one confirmation per order. An Err publishes nothing and settles the whole batch with its outcome.
documents.s: A batch's replies in one block

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm.batch(nonzero!(32))) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish) .transactional() .include(ship) .out(Shipments, TransactionalPublish) }) } src/main.rs fn service(broker: RedisBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let confirm = subscriber(RedisStream::new("orders").group("confirmations"), Confirm); let ship = subscriber(RedisStream::new("packed").group("shipping"), Ship); b.include(confirm.batch(nonzero!(32)).reply().build()) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish) .transactional() .include(ship.build()) .out(Shipments, TransactionalPublish) }) } .out_reply(TransactionalPublish).transactional() asks for the borrowed kind. The runtime opens a transaction on the reply publisher, publishes the batch's replies into it and commits. TransactionalPublish is RedisTransactionalPublish under the stream prelude's name. It sends with XADD, like Publish, and runs only where transactions run. The size of the batch is the COUNT of the read that fetches it, so one transaction holds at most 32 confirmations here.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Publishes one shipment per item of a parcel, committed as one block. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("packed").group("shipping"))] async fn ship( parcel: &Parcel, Out(shipments): Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(mut transaction) = shipments.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; for item in &parcel.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(parcel.order_id, "a nameless item, the parcel ships nothing"); // The abort discards the shipments buffered so far. return match transaction.abort().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), }; } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: parcel.order_id, item: item.clone(), }; if transaction.message(&shipment).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } } match transaction.commit().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } src/main.rs /// Publishes one shipment per item of a parcel, committed as one block. struct Ship; impl<Slot> Handle<Parcel, (), Outs<(Slot,)>> for Ship where Slot: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: OwnedTransactions>, { async fn handle( &self, parcel: &Parcel, outs: &Outs<(Slot,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut transaction = outs .get(Shipments) .transaction() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; for item in &parcel.items { if item.is_empty() { tracing::warn!(parcel.order_id, "a nameless item, the parcel ships nothing"); // The abort discards the shipments buffered so far. transaction .abort() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } let shipment = Shipment { order_id: parcel.order_id, item: item.clone(), }; transaction .message(&shipment) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; } transaction .commit() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } transaction() on an Out slot returns a value that owns its buffer. Its publishes go into the buffer, commit sends the buffer as one block, and abort discards it. commit and abort consume the value, so a second commit or a publish after the end does not compile. Several owned transactions can be open on one publisher at once, and settling one never touches another. A transaction dropped without either is discarded like an abort, with a warning in the log. owned_transaction() is the same over values: each publish takes a destination and a value and encodes it with the default codec. It suits a startup hook, such as after_startup, that seeds a stream.

Redis queues the commands of a block and runs them together; it does not undo them. A command the server refuses to queue, such as one with a wrong number of arguments, discards the whole block, and commit returns an error. A command that fails while the block runs leaves the commands before it applied. For a group of XADDs that happens when the server runs out of memory or a key holds another type. A failed commit has consumed its transaction, and the buffer is gone. The handler returns retry, and the delivery comes again and builds a new transaction.

Transactions run on a standalone server and on a sentinel deployment. A MULTI block cannot span hash slots, so on a cluster a service that mounts TransactionalPublish does not start. The list and Pub/Sub publishers have no transactions. A transaction covers publishes. On the consuming side, .pipeline().atomic() puts a handler's own Redis commands and the acknowledgement of its delivery in one block.

The tests in the example files run in process, where the in-process Redis runs MULTI and EXEC. They check that a batch's confirmations and a parcel's shipments arrive together, and that a dropped batch and an aborted parcel publish nothing. One more test starts the same service with a cluster broker and checks that it does not start.

This guide runs a work queue on a Redis list, from a simple queue to a reliable one that recovers the jobs of a stopped worker. The example is an image service. It warms its page cache from one queue and renders thumbnails from another.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "cache.warmups")] struct Warmup { page: String, } #[subscriber(RedisList::new("cache.warmups"))] async fn warm_cache(warmup: &Warmup) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(warmup.page, "page cached"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Warmup { page: String, } outgoing!(Warmup, "cache.warmups"); struct WarmCache; impl Handle<Warmup> for WarmCache { fn handle( &self, warmup: &Warmup, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(warmup.page, "page cached"); ready(Ok(())) } } A producer pushes an entry onto the left of a list with LPUSH. RedisList::new pops from the right with BRPOP, so entries come out in the order they went in, and each one reaches exactly one consumer. Every running instance of the service pops from the same list, so the instances share the work. The pop removes the entry from Redis before the handler runs. If the service stops while the handler runs, the entry is gone. The queue delivers each entry at most once, and the handler's outcome settles nothing. A missed cache warmup costs one slow page, so cache.warmups is a simple queue.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// Longer than the slowest render ever takes: a claim idle this long belongs to no live worker. const MIN_IDLE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct ThumbnailJob { image: String, } #[subscriber( RedisList::new("{thumbnails}") .reliable() .min_idle(MIN_IDLE) .recovery_zset("{thumbnails}.claims") )] async fn render(job: &ThumbnailJob) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(job.image, "thumbnail rendered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// Longer than the slowest render ever takes: a claim idle this long belongs to no live worker. const MIN_IDLE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(60); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct ThumbnailJob { image: String, } outgoing!(ThumbnailJob); struct Render; impl Handle<ThumbnailJob> for Render { fn handle( &self, job: &ThumbnailJob, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(job.image, "thumbnail rendered"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn thumbnails() -> RedisList { RedisList::new("{thumbnails}") .reliable() .min_idle(MIN_IDLE) .recovery_zset("{thumbnails}.claims") } reliable moves each entry to a processing list in one command, BLMOVE, instead of popping it. The processing list is {thumbnails}.processing, the queue's key with .processing after it, unless processing names another. The entry stays there while the handler runs: ack removes it from the processing list with LREM; retry moves it back to the queue; drop removes it. So a job leaves Redis only once a handler has finished with it, and the queue delivers each entry at least once.

A worker that stops between the move and the acknowledgement leaves its entry on the processing list. A list keeps no record of who took an entry or when, so nothing returns it on its own. recovery_zset turns on a watchdog for that. Each move records the entry in a sorted set, scored by the time it was taken, and the acknowledgement removes the record. As the subscription reads, it moves every entry idle longer than min_idle back onto the queue, where any worker can take it. min_idle is required with the recovery set, and a subscription without it does not start. Set it above the longest time a job ever takes: a shorter value takes a job away from a worker that is still on it, and the thumbnail is rendered twice. recovery_ttl expires an abandoned recovery set, and has to be longer than min_idle. The scores are wall-clock milliseconds, so the clocks of the service's hosts need to agree.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "uploads")] struct Upload { image: String, } // Braces in `#[outgoing(name = ..)]` read as a name template, so the mount site names the key. #[subscriber(RedisStream::new("uploads").group("thumbnailer"), reply("{thumbnails}"))] async fn queue_thumbnail(upload: &Upload) -> ThumbnailJob { ThumbnailJob { image: upload.image.clone(), } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Upload { image: String, } outgoing!(Upload, "uploads"); struct QueueThumbnail; impl Handle<Upload, ThumbnailJob> for QueueThumbnail { fn handle( &self, upload: &Upload, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<ThumbnailJob, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(ThumbnailJob { image: upload.image.clone(), })) } } queue_thumbnail reads uploads off a stream and answers each one with a thumbnail job. The job goes to {thumbnails}, which the mount site names. A name in #[outgoing(name = ..)] reads braces as a name template, so a key with a hash tag is named at the mount site instead. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("images", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(warm_cache) .include(render) // A queue nobody fed for a day expires, with whatever is left in it. .include(queue_thumbnail) .out_reply(list::Publish::new().ttl(Duration::from_hours(24))) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("images", "0.1.0")).with_broker( RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(RedisList::new("cache.warmups"), WarmCache).build()) .include(subscriber(thumbnails(), Render).build()) // A queue nobody fed for a day expires, with whatever is left in it. .include( subscriber( RedisStream::new("uploads").group("thumbnailer"), QueueThumbnail, ) .reply() .to("{thumbnails}") .build(), ) .out_reply(list::Publish::new().ttl(Duration::from_hours(24))) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The reply leaves through list::Publish, which pushes with LPUSH. Its ttl re-arms an expiry on the queue's key at every push. A queue in use never expires, and a queue nobody fed for a day lapses with whatever it still holds. A list has no per-entry expiry, so the expiry always covers the whole queue.

On a cluster, a reliable queue and its processing list have to live on one hash slot, because one command moves an entry between them. A hash tag gives them one: Redis hashes only the part of the key inside the braces, so {thumbnails} and {thumbnails}.processing land on the same node. A reliable queue whose two keys land on different slots does not start, and the error names the hash tag to use. The example names its keys with a tag already, so it moves to a cluster unchanged.

A list keeps no history: an entry that was handled is gone, and no second service can read it too. The recovery watchdog is the only redelivery a list has, and a list has no delivery count of its own. When several services read the same work, when the work needs replay, or when a stopped worker's job must come back without a watchdog, use a stream with a consumer group, as Consumer groups and crash recovery shows. The tests in the example file publish a warmup and an upload and check what the handlers received. One moves the clock past min_idle and checks that a rendered job does not come back.
